body: The pipes in the wall knock first, the shower at the far end of the hall working its way toward hot, and under the knocking Theo’s iPhone chimes on the desk: one note, a gap, one note, a gap. Past the blind the quad is still gray, under a fog that hasn’t decided to leave.

The navy blazer is a pledge’s blazer now and not a rushee’s, and Theo sits at the desk in it. The bid card from last night stands against the lamp exactly where it stood at ten to midnight. Beside it on the blotter lies a small gold pin, shaped like a sword or an anchor (it has been explained to Theo, under oath, and he can’t say which), and beside the pin sits a white china teacup with a raw egg in it, HOLLIS lettered down the shell in blue ballpoint capitals, in somebody else’s hand.
“Don’t,” Theo says, without turning around.
Jack, up on one elbow, hasn’t said a word.

“Brooks’s assignment. I carry him everywhere for a week. He’s named for a founder, the same Hollis as the building, somebody’s great-great-uncle, a man who sat on a railroad board and held an opinion on everything else. There is a sheet of rules. He may be presented at meals. He is back in the cup by noon.” Theo looks at the cup. “If it breaks, I’m out. If it hatches, I’m president.”
“Is that shower ever going to be hot?” Jack says.

“That shower has not been hot at this hour since the Eisenhower administration. It’s an exercise in hope.” Theo straightens a cuff. “Tuesday I ate an onion. Thursday I carry an egg. By the end of the month, I’m told, I will be required to love a man named Bucky.”
“What do you do when you sleep?” Jack says.

“He sleeps on the nightstand, in the cup, and I sleep with one ear open. The rules are silent on what happens to a pledge who rolls over.” Theo sighs through his nose. “Picture it: a boy, an egg, a week. Altman would have shot it in one take and wept in the car.”

The phone is propped against the base of the lamp with CNN on it, the sound low: the airport at Port-au-Prince from the air, one runway, planes circling in a line over the water and pallets stacking up on a tarmac with no way to send them into the city. One plane comes down out of the stack while Jack watches, and the rest go on circling. Theo’s thumb goes. The chime comes back.

“Text YES to confirm your ten-dollar donation to the American Red Cross,” he reads, to the lamp. “Yes.” The thumb. The chime. By the time Jack has his feet on the cold floor Theo has done it ten times, and he reads the tenth in the voice he used for the first.

“A hundred dollars,” he says, “in ten-dollar increments, because the phone company insists on a ritual. It goes on my father’s statement. A woman in his office will open it and feel something on his behalf.”
“You could write a check,” Jack says.
“A check is a decision. This is a practice.”
“It’ll take more than ten dollars,” Jack says.
“It’ll take ten dollars from everybody.” Theo says it short, to the screen, where another plane has begun its circuit. “So I’m being everybody. Ten times.”

He picks up the phone again, and this time it’s the other thing, the text that came in while Jack slept. “Seven-twelve,” Theo reads, off the screen, flat. “*he got his bid. good for him.*” He sets the phone down on the blotter. “Congratulations from Laney. In the third person. I’m told that’s progress.”
“She’s texting you,” Jack says.
“She’s texting *at* me. It’s a distinction she insists on.” Then he takes the phone up again and goes to Jack’s wall (he can see it, being a friend) and reports on it like news from a distant front.
“Thirty-one new friends since Tuesday. I counted. One of them is a dentist.”
From the wall he goes to the News Feed, and down it with one thumb.
The thumb stops. He looks across the room at Jack, and keeps looking, with the phone lit in his hand. “Hollis has to be back in the cup by noon,” he says. “Those are the rules.” And scrolls on.

At the mirror on the inside of the closet door he pins the pin to his lapel. Under Jack’s pillow the RAZR buzzes, and Jack’s hand is under there before the second buzz, because that is where it lives now. In the glass Theo’s eyes follow the hand out from under the pillow and come back to the lapel. The pin is straight. He says nothing about it.

body: At seven fifty-two, because Brooks holds that punctuality is a form of love, Theo lifts the teacup off the blotter in both hands, level, and gets as far as the door before he sees the problem. The door has a knob, and he has no hand.

choices.text: “What’s his middle name?”
response: “Ashby,” Theo says. “He’s family now.” He gets the knob with his elbow, a skill he must have practiced in the night, and the cup goes out ahead of him into the hall, where the shower pipes are still knocking.

choices.text: “Congratulations. Really.”
response: Theo stops with the cup half through the doorway. He doesn’t turn around. “I owe you a kidney,” he says, short, and goes, and his footsteps take the cup down the hall at a walk Jack has never seen on him, slow and even and entirely without style.

choices.text: *Get the door for him.*
response: Jack gets there first and holds it. Theo goes through sideways, cup first, like a man carrying a candle in a wind, and goes down the hall with it, and the door stays open on the long carpet and the knocking pipes.

body: The south wall of Morro 1100 is glass from the floor to the ceiling, and at eleven the sun comes through it low and lies across the bottom rows in bright bars, so the people down front sit in weather and the back row sits in shade. Up in the shade, in the corner seat under the exit sign, Skye has the hood up and the sunglasses on and her feet on the seat in front of her, and the seat beside her has *Oceanography 1* on it, keeping his place.
She lifts the book off the seat as he comes down the last step and sets it in his lap when he sits, like a napkin. “You sat where you sat,” she says. “I’m so proud of you.”

Fenner comes on at eleven exactly, in the Tevas, with the coffee, and doesn’t bother with a slide. “Look to your left,” he says into the microphone. “Look to your right. One of those people is your partner till May. The other one is a stranger, and will stay one.” He drinks. “Seats are partners. If you’re sitting next to somebody you hate, you should have thought of that Tuesday.”

A groan goes up out of three hundred people at once, low and long: the sound of a lecture hall finding out. The back row doesn’t groan. In the middle rows a boy in a fraternity sweatshirt has his hand in the air before Fenner is done.
“No,” Fenner says. “No trades. I have heard every reason. I have heard a death in the family on behalf of a goldfish.”
Skye takes her feet down off the seat in front and turns to him and holds out her hand, very formal, as if they’re closing on a house. He shakes it.
“A partner I can’t get fired,” she says. “This is going to be so good for me.”

The project, Fenner says, is one question you can answer by May with the ocean, a library card and each other, turned in on a half-sheet before you leave this room. And not — he holds up a hand — *why is the ocean*. “I’ve had *why is the ocean*. I gave it a C. It was a kind C.”

Skye has her answer before he’s finished saying it. She doesn’t write it down. She takes the pencil out of Jack’s hand and draws, on the legal pad on his desk: a hook of land, a dark lump off the end of it for the reef, and the swell coming in from the top of the page in long straight lines that bend as they reach the lump and wrap around it toward the land.

“Refraction,” she says, and it’s the right word, used right. “The part of the wave that gets to the reef first feels the bottom and slows down, and the rest of it keeps going, so the line bends in. A marching band turning a corner. The inside guys take tiny steps.” She taps the lump with the pencil. “That’s why the Point breaks where it does. The reef’s a lens. It aims every wave that comes in at the same rocks.”
He looks at her.
“I read the chapter,” she says. “Twice. Once for me and once for Cassidy. Cassidy’s very behind in school.”
So she draws and he writes. He tears the sheet down the middle so they’ll each have a half, and copies it out on both, and spells it himself, every letter, without looking over at her.

body.title: A half-sheet, torn from a legal pad
body.text:
PAIR 41 — CALLENDER / COSTIGAN
QUESTION: Why does the Point break where it does?
(bathymetry. refraction. the reef.)

body: In his margin, before he can stop her, in capitals: *ITS A SCIENCE*. And under it, smaller, so he has to lean in to read it: *still yes*.

Fenner comes up the aisle collecting slips, and when he gets to the back row he reads theirs standing over them with the coffee in his other hand. He takes in the hood, the sunglasses and the kid from Ohio, in that order. “The Point,” he says. He doesn’t give it back. “Approved. Don’t drown. Nobody gets an extension for drowning.”

She writes in his margin while Fenner goes down the far aisle: *he has a boat named after his first wife*. He writes back *how do you know*. She writes *nobody names a boat after the second one*, and caps her pen on it.
When he has gone back down the stairs Skye says, without moving her mouth much: “We need data.”
“We have a library card.”

“We need *field* data. Saturday. Before light. I’m taking you out again.” Under the little desk her knee comes over against his. “Not the Point. The Point would kill you. The Point is for guys whose mothers have stopped calling. The inside. There’s white water on the sand south of the reef, and you can fall down in it all morning, and the worst thing out there is me.”
“What time?”
“Saturday starts at six.” She writes it in his margin, a *6* with a circle around it. “Bring your face.”

Two rows down a girl has her phone up again, at the angle that’s supposed to look like she’s checking the time. Skye gives her a thumbs-up without turning her head from Fenner. The phone goes down. After a minute it comes back up.

journal.title: Oceanography 1
journal.text: Oceanography 1, Tuesdays and Thursdays at eleven, Morro Hall 1100. Rocks for Jocks, Wet. Skye took it too and didn’t tell me which science till she was sitting in the back row under the exit sign with the book. Fenner: seventy-one percent, and we have better maps of Mars. The ground is not where you left it, week two. Partners by seat, Thursday. Till May. No trades. Thursday: partners by seat. Skye, till May. Our project is the Point — why it breaks where it does. Fenner: approved, don’t drown.

choices.text: “I’m going to be terrible.”
response: “You’re going to be terrible on the inside,” Skye says. “That’s what the inside is for.”
“And the outside?”
“The outside is where I watch.” She props her chin on her hand and looks at him over the sunglasses. “I’m very supportive from the outside.”

Down front Fenner says *Tuesday, chapter four*, and the hall gets up all at once in a crash of fold-down desks. She folds her half of the sheet in quarters, puts it in the front pocket of the hoodie and pats it to make sure it’s there.

choices.text: “If I drown, you get the A.”
response: “If you drown I get a very moving A.” She writes it in his margin — *A (MOVING)* — and draws a small halo over it. “I’ll read something at the service. Fenner will cry into the coffee.”
“You’d get an extension.”
“Not for drowning,” Skye says, in Fenner’s Texas, and he has to put his head down on the little desk.
When the hall stands up she keeps her half of the sheet, folded small in the pocket of the hoodie, and goes up the stairs ahead of him into the noon with one hand held out behind her for his.

choices.text: *Draw her the reef in the margin, from above.*
response: He takes the pencil back and draws it for her the way the land actually lies, from above: the hook of the Point, the dirt lot at the end of Seacliff, the reef as a long dark tongue under the water, and south of it the sand bar, with the white water running in over it in scallops. He can draw a coastline. He copied six Lents of maps off the sides of Rice Bowl boxes. She watches the pencil the whole time, and when he’s done she takes it from him and writes *YOU* in the white water, with an arrow.
When the hall stands up she tears the corner with the drawing off his page and keeps it with her half of the sheet, both of them folded together into the hoodie pocket.

body: At one o’clock the window end of Hollis 302 is full of light off the eucalyptus, and the door end, under the clock, isn’t. Lena is at the window end already. She has the last chair, the one with its back to the glass, and she has been in it long enough to have her *Frankenstein* out and lined up with the edge of the table and a pencil pushed through her hair. The gray cardigan, buttoned to the throat. Every other chair is still pushed in.
She looks up when the door opens, sees who it is, and goes back to her page.
Jack takes the chair at the door end, under the clock, and puts his bag down against his leg. The corner chair beside his stays pushed in.

For a minute it’s the two of them and the radiator. She turns a page. The radiator knocks twice, the way it did all fall, and neither of them says the thing either of them would have said about it in October. He gets his own copy out. There are his margins from Christmas, in his own hand, arguing with Victor; he can’t make one of them mean anything.

The rest come in by twos. Caleb Hargrove has fringed his paperback with Post-its in four colors and takes the chair nearest the middle, where Hale will be. Evan Marsh, Hale’s reader, has already put a photocopy at every place — Volume One, chapters seven and eight — and sits at the side with his notebook open and his pen uncapped. Yusuf comes in last with a coffee, looks at the empty corner by Jack, and takes it because it’s there.

“The bench grinder came home Tuesday,” he says, working the lid off. “And his good calipers. My mother started a second shelf.” He blows across the coffee. It’s information; he doesn’t want anything for it. Jack nods. Yusuf nods back and drinks.
Hale comes in at seven past with the novel shut on one finger and no dog. He stops inside the door and looks down the length of the table, from Jack to the window, and back.
“Someone listened,” he says.
He takes his own chair halfway down the long side, where he can’t see either end without turning his head, and he turns it all hour.

“Mary Shelley was eighteen when she began this book,” he says, “which ought to shame every one of you. The trial of Justine Moritz.” He lays the book open on the table. “A little boy is strangled in a field outside Geneva. A servant girl is found with the miniature he was wearing in her pocket. She is tried, convicted and hanged. In the courtroom sits Victor Frankenstein, who knows exactly who did it, because he built him. He could explain the business in a sentence. He doesn’t.” He looks at the window end, and then at the door. “Coward, or realist?”

For most of an hour the table takes it apart. Caleb has Victor’s own excuse flagged in green — he’d have been taken for a madman, he says so on the page — and reads it out as if that settles it. Yusuf says Victor never thinks about the girl once that isn’t really about Victor, and Hale makes him find the line, and he finds it: *the tortures of the accused did not equal mine.* Somebody along the window side laughs, not kindly. Lena says, once, to Hale, that Victor had all the proof a court could want — he had himself — and goes back to listening. Evan writes all of it down.
When Caleb says Victor should have lawyered up, the corner of her mouth goes, at Hale, and comes back where it was. It doesn’t go anywhere near the door end.

“Victor calls himself the true murderer,” Hale observes, “once she’s safely dead and it costs him nothing. Realism, ladies and gentlemen, is the name a coward gives his arithmetic. Discuss.” Caleb writes it on a yellow Post-it, and then, after some thought, moves it to the green.
Hale has sat back with his hands folded over the novel. He doesn’t referee. He seems to have been waiting all January for this, and to want it to go on.
With ten minutes left he turns his head toward the door. “Mr. Costigan. You’ve been very quiet. In you it’s a symptom.”

“Victor’s right,” Jack says. “Nobody would have believed him. He stands up in that courtroom and says a thing he sewed together out of graves did it, and they walk him out to an asylum, and she hangs the same morning anyway. The sentence doesn’t save her. It just damns him with her.”
At the far end Lena pushes the sleeves of the cardigan up to the elbow.

“Elizabeth didn’t have any proof either.” Lena says it from the far end of the table, to Hale, with her eyes on Hale. “She stood up in front of the court and spoke for that girl. She had nothing to give but her word for who Justine was, and she gave it, with all of Geneva looking at her.”
“And they hanged Justine anyway,” Jack says. “Elizabeth said it out loud and it didn’t move one of them. The book tells you exactly what the sentence was worth.”
“The book tells you what *Victor* was worth.” Her pencil goes down on the table, flat, lined up with the book. “That’s what everybody who says nothing tells himself. *Nobody would have believed me.*”
Her hand has gone to the medal at her collar. It closes on it through the gray wool and holds it there.
Jack sees her hand before he knows about his own. His is flat on the front of his shirt, over the St. Michael underneath, and he couldn’t say since when. He puts it on the table.
“Well,” Hale says, and turns his head back toward the door. “Coward, or realist, Mr. Costigan? Take your time. Miss Broussard has taken hers.”

choices.text: “Nobody would have believed him. They’d have hanged her and locked him up.”
choices.key: At Hale’s table you argued Victor was right to keep quiet: nobody would have believed him.
response: “Nobody would have believed him,” Jack says. “They’d have hanged her and locked him up.”
“Then he’d have been locked up telling the truth,” Lena says, to her page.

Hale caps his pen. “Miss Broussard, you are prosecuting silence. Mr. Costigan, you are defending it.” He looks from one end of the table to the other, and seems to like each of them a little less and the hour a good deal more. “Three pages each on why you are wrong. Thursday.”
Caleb writes THURSDAY on a pink Post-it and sticks it inside his cover. At the window end Lena has already started; the pencil has come out of her hair, and it’s going.
When the chairs go back she has to pass his to reach the door. She does it with the novel held flat against her chest. “Thursday,” she says, to the door, and goes down the stairs ahead of everybody.

choices.text: “He should have said it. He knew. That’s the whole sin.”
choices.key: At Hale’s table you gave Lena the point: Victor knew, and should have said it.
response: “He should have said it,” Jack says. “He knew. That’s the whole sin.”

At the far end Lena looks down the length of the table at him, straight, for the first time since Hale sat down. She doesn’t say anything. She looks long enough that Yusuf stops with the coffee halfway up, and then she looks back at her book.

“Mr. Costigan has defected,” Hale says. “How disappointing for everyone. Miss Broussard, you are still prosecuting silence. Mr. Costigan, you will defend it anyway, in writing, against your own conscience, which will do you good. Three pages each on why you are wrong. Thursday.”

The chairs go back. She passes his on her way to the door with the novel against her chest, and slows, and for a moment he thinks she’s going to say something. She says, “Yusuf, your lid,” and Yusuf catches his coffee before it goes.

choices.text: “Then look at the priest who made her confess to it.”
choices.key: At Hale’s table you turned it to Justine’s confessor, who scared her into a false confession.
response: “Then look at the priest,” Jack says. “The one who heard her confession. She didn’t do it, and he kept at her with excommunication and hell till she said she did.” He finds it on Evan’s photocopy, her own words in the cell: her confessor *threatened and menaced*, until she almost began to think she was the monster he said she was. “She went to the gallows absolved of a murder she never committed. Victor kept quiet. That man made her lie.”
“Then the priest’s a monster too,” Lena says.
“That’s not confession. That’s a man who wanted a verdict.”

Hale looks at him as if somebody has brought him a present he didn’t expect and is going to enjoy unwrapping. “Three pages each on why you are wrong,” he says. “Thursday. Mr. Costigan may include the clergy.”

Yusuf, packing up, says quietly to Jack, “My uncle would like your priest,” and doesn’t explain. At the window end Lena is writing something in her margin, fast, and doesn’t stop when the room empties around her.

choices.text: “Easy to say from the far end of the table.”
choices.key: At Hale’s table you told Lena it was easy to say from the far end.
response: “Easy to say,” Jack says, “from the far end of the table.”
Lena’s voice goes formal and pleasant, every word in its place. “I sat where I was told, Jack.”
Caleb peels a Post-it off his pad very slowly, so it won’t make a sound, and it makes one anyway.
“Three pages each on why you are wrong,” Hale says. “Thursday.” He shuts the book. “Keep the seating.”
Lena goes out first, past his chair, without slowing down. Yusuf puts the lid back on his coffee and doesn’t look at anyone.

journal.title: Kevin Tran
journal.text: Kevin Tran. Goes to daily Mass, saves you a seat with a Bible. Has a sister, Tina, in dental school, who flossed in the womb. Lies to his mom about orgo in Vietnamese. Drives his mother’s Odyssey at sixty-five, not sixty-six. His dad has two nail-salon supply stores in San Jose and has never had a Labor Day. Brought six pairs of gloves to a beach cleanup. Mouthed every word of Joey’s first reading from the second pew. Somebody coached Joey; I can guess who. Brought tea to a wake. His Bà Nội says heaven makes the elephant and heaven makes the grass. Walked Margot down at four in the morning. Handed Lena a roll of quarters for the payphone before she asked. Halloween: All Saints, every one nobody’s heard of — scrubs, a halo and a white mask. He found Laney. Friday night a pre-med said Maine got it right. Kevin answered him and went to get water. Tuesday, the Vietnamese Martyrs: his mother reads eleven of the hundred and seventeen. Asked about the scar. Alarm Five, on the lawn: he had a question mark next to my name on his clipboard. I told Priya I was out. He erased it. Tuesday at four I woke him for Doug. A chair under the knob, then a bell. Wednesday at the Brick, at the next carrel all night: ‘You two have been defending each other for three hours. That isn’t studying.’ Sings bass. A real one. Seven years of Vietnamese choir in San Jose — his mother made him. Friday, from the Odyssey: Go home. Sleep. Tell somebody something. Back from San Jose. His mother has a girl from their parish she wants him to call. Clare. She plays the violin in the Mass band. Wednesday he brought two flats of water to the Haiti table, which nobody asked for, and stayed to hold Clare’s violin case. ‘My mother knows your mother.’ Thursday he called Clare. His mother had the number, and his grandmother was on the speaker. She said yes to Sully’s.

body: Sundown was at eight past five, and the lounge has been left with what it leaves: the vending machine’s one lit face, the window gone to blue ink, and Doug Pruitt’s laptop on the coffee table throwing the only other light, CNN.com with the sound off. On the screen a street in Port-au-Prince has become a hill, and there are people standing on the hill. Behind it the whiteboard waits on its wheeled stand, COSTIGAN | BROUSSARD down the middle in Margot’s marks, months old and never wiped.

Doug is cross-legged on the couch with his phone in both hands. “Forty,” he announces, as the last chime comes back, and reads it off the screen. “YES.” He lowers the phone. “That’s four hundred dollars, dude. My dad’s going to see the bill and think I joined a cult.”
“Forty texts, Douglas,” says Margot, from the armchair, without looking up from her legal pad. “A cult has a leader. This is a novena with a carrier.”
“Every one of them is a yes, though,” Doug says. He means it; his face has gone earnest. “I said yes forty times to something. When’s the last time I did that?”
“Yesterday,” says Margot, “to the cheesecake.”

Jack has come up for his Anchor shirt, drying on the radiator since Tuesday for reasons the fourth floor has stopped asking about. It is still damp at the collar. He is due on the Hobart at eight. He takes it down.
Doug flips a tab, off the hill and onto his News Feed, and frowns at it. “Kayla Ruiz is now friends with Kenzie Rourke. Who’s Kenzie Rourke?”
“The cantor,” Jack says.
“Why is that on my feed?”
“Because it’s a network, Douglas,” Margot says. “Everyone is on everyone’s feed. That is what the word means.”

At the far end of the couch Kevin has his BlackBerry face-up on his knee, and it lights: a text from his mother, a name and a 408 number and nothing else, no greeting, no punctuation. Mrs. Tran texts the way she wires money. Before he can touch it, the phone is ringing on his knee, and out of habit he thumbs the speaker, and the lounge fills up with two women at once.
“Minh? You got the number?”
Another voice comes in over hers in Vietnamese, fast, until the little speaker crackles, and then it arrives in English, complete and satisfied. “She plays the violin for God, Minh.”
“For the *church*,” his mother says, behind her.
“Same building.”
Kevin sits up at *Minh* the way he sits up for no one else, and answers: “Dạ. Dạ, Bà Nội. Dạ.”
Doug leans over the arm of the couch toward Jack and says, in a stage whisper, “He’s only got the one, dude. He just says it with different feelings.”
The call ends in something warm and final in two voices, and a last *dạ*, and the BlackBerry goes quiet in Kevin’s hand. He stands there holding a number.

Margot has put down the pad. “Call her now,” she says, in a voice Jack can’t read. “If you wait you will rehearse, and it will sound rehearsed. Impression management, Kevin. Establish the frame early—”
“I’m *managing*.”

“You are sweating through a polo.” She turns a page she isn’t reading. “Open with the mothers; they are your only shared fact. Do not mention the violin. She has heard about the violin every day of her life from people who can’t play one.”
“I wasn’t going to mention the violin.”
“You had it in your mouth. Ask her about something that isn’t her.”

He goes to the window to do it, with his back to the room. Clare’s voice comes out of the BlackBerry as a small bright sound, the shape of a question, and Kevin’s half is all there is: “Hi — Clare? It’s Kevin Tran. We met at — at the table. With the water. Our mothers — yes. Yes, they do. They do know each other.” He turns around and aims his face at the ceiling. “Okay, so, there’s a football thing. Saturday. It’s for a friend from New Orleans, it’s the Saints, it’s a playoff game. She moved it — it’s not in the Fishbowl anymore. It’s at Sully’s, on Mission. There’s food. There are also pitchers, but there’s food.”
Jack is standing with the damp shirt over one arm and the RAZR in his other hand, where his thumb has been working the cracked hinge open and shut. The thumb stops.
The small bright sound again. “Yes?” Kevin says. “Yes. Okay. Okay, great.” He takes the phone from his ear and looks at it, as if it could explain what has just happened to him.
“You said *playoff game* like it was on a box, dude,” Doug says, with admiration.
“She said yes,” he reports to the lounge. Then, after a moment: “She said she has four brothers.”
“Four brothers is a favorable finding,” Margot says. “It means she has seen the worst of the species at close range and answered the phone anyway.”

choices.text: “She said yes, Kev. That’s the whole thing.”
response: Kevin nods slowly, as if handed a diagnosis he can live with. “Okay,” he says. “Yes. That’s the whole thing.”
Doug, from the couch, wants to know if the brothers are the kind who ask what your intentions are or the kind who just stand there.
“It’s the same kind, Douglas,” Margot says. “There is only the one.”

choices.text: “Four brothers. Wear a cup.”
response: Margot laughs into her legal pad, a single bark, and is furious about it.
Kevin turns the BlackBerry over in his hands. “That’s — respectfully — not the sport,” he says, and then, to the window, quieter, “but I’ll look into it.”

choices.text: “You okay?”
response: Kevin gives him the smile, the team-captain one, all the way up. “I’m great,” he says. “I have a plan and a number.” Margot watches him say it, and the pad stays down on her knee.

body: The Hobart takes a rack with a slam and then the long climbing hiss of the wash, and over the hiss Rudy scrapes the flat-top down in four hard strokes, and by the door somebody has fed the jukebox a quarter. It’s Otis Redding, slow, with the horns breathing behind him: 1962, out of a speaker that was old in 1980.
Jack comes on at eight. Gloria is at the pass tying her apron behind her back when he comes in from the alley with his shirt still damp at the collar.
“Tuesday you called,” she says. “Haiti. That’s a pass.”
“Thank you.”
She pulls the bow tight. “Whatever you ask me for next, that one’s a favor.”
“I’m not asking for anything.”
“Not yet, hon.”

The corner booth already has Margot in it, with a *Tide* reporter’s notebook open beside her coffee and three pens laid out above it in a row, and across from her, in his flannel with the cuffs rolled, Skye. They came in at ten to, Rudy says, and asked for the booth with a view of the dishwasher. On her way back from the register Gloria stops at the pie case, cuts a slice of boysenberry nobody has ordered, sets it down in front of Skye without a word, and keeps going. Skye looks at the slice, and at Gloria’s back, and through the pass at Jack, and puts a hand over her heart.
He gets the interview in pieces. That’s all the Hobart allows. He busses the counter and runs racks, and every time he comes out with the tub he catches another piece of it.

“—Goffman,” Margot is saying. “Front stage and back stage. The front stage is where the performance happens. The back stage is where the performer can finally drop the—” and the Hobart comes down on the next rack, and the rest of it goes into the steam.

When he’s out again Skye is answering a question he didn’t hear, in a voice that isn’t hers: slow and flat, a hostage reading off a card. “I am being treated well. I have been given coffee.” Then, as herself: “A cereal commercial. I was six. I had to love a raisin. I loved it so hard they ran the take for two years.”
Margot writes. “And the self underneath. The one in the dressing room.”

“There’s no backstage,” Skye says. “That’s the trick. There are just more stages.” She takes a forkful of the pie. “The dressing room is a stage. The car is a stage. My mother’s kitchen is the hardest room to play in Los Angeles.”
“Goffman would call that a very backstage thing to say.”
“Goffman thinks you’re lying when you perform,” Skye says. “Actors think you’re lying when you don’t. If I came in here with no face on, you’d write that I was *withholding*.”
Margot’s pen stops. “I would,” she says. “I’d underline it.”
On the next pass Margot has the pen held up like a cigarette. “How many selves would you say, on a weekday?”
“Four.” Skye doesn’t have to think. “Five on Thursdays. Cassidy’s on at nine.”

He’s wiping down the next booth over when Margot asks about him. He knows it’s about him because her eyes come up off the notebook to the boy in the dish apron with the wet rag and rest on him. “And Costigan,” she says. “How many is he?”
Skye doesn’t turn around. “One,” she says. “He’s the only person I’ve ever met who’s the same in every room. It’s very annoying. I keep checking.”
The booth goes quiet after that. Jack wipes the same table twice and takes the tub back through the swinging door.
When he comes out again with a rack of cups she’s at the pass, waiting for him, with her elbows on the steel shelf under the heat lamps. Customers don’t stand there.
“You heard that,” she says.
“I heard that.”

“Good. Now it’s in the paper.” She reaches through and turns his apron strap right side out where it’s twisted at his neck, and leaves her fingers on his collar after it’s fixed, and then goes back to the booth.

Next time through, they’ve got to faith. “—also a stage,” Margot is saying. “Ritual is the most stage-managed thing human beings do. Costumes. Lighting. A script that hasn’t been revised since Trent.”
“It’s not his stage,” Skye says. “I don’t believe it. I believe *he* does. Those are different, and the second one is very attractive.”
Margot looks at her across the pie for some time.
“I hate that that was good,” she says, and then writes it.

The white phone lights up on the table between the coffee cups a little after nine. Skye looks at the name and turns the screen to show Margot, and Margot says, “Take it. I’ll interview the pie,” and Skye slides out of the booth and takes it out onto the wharf.

He watches her through the window over the sink. Out there, under the last lamp before the bait shack, she walks with the phone at her ear and her free arm wrapped around herself in his flannel, ten steps up the planks and ten steps back. He can’t hear any of it, and he doesn’t try to read her mouth. Partway through she stops dead and looks down at the black water and laughs at it, a laugh he can see from inside, and starts walking again. The Hobart finishes its cycle and he has to look down to pull the rack.
While she’s out there Margot brings her own cup up to the pass instead of waiting on Gloria and holds it through the window at Jack, who is not the waitress, until he fills it off the warmer.
“She’s the only interesting person you’ve ever dated, Costigan,” Margot says. “Which is an indictment.”
“Of who?”
“Yes,” says Margot, and takes her coffee back to the pie.
She comes in at half past with her cheeks red from the wind and stops at the bus station by the pass, where he’s stacking clean cups, instead of going back to the booth.

“Sunday night,” she says. “The network’s Golden Globes party. A hotel in Beverly Hills. I go alone, as Cassidy, in something they send over, and I smile at everybody who has ever signed a check, and Corinne doesn’t put out a statement about Haiti with my name on it. And nothing new goes up. On my page. Till she says.”
“It’s a trade.”
“It’s a trade.”

“She wanted the statement more than she wanted me home on a Sunday,” Skye says. “I wanted no statement more than I wanted the Sunday. So everybody loses the thing they can stand to lose. That’s a negotiation.”
“Is it a good one?”

Skye takes a clean spoon off the top of his stack and looks at herself upside down in it. “It’s a party,” she says. “I’ll steal you a mint.” She puts the spoon back, and with the thumb of the same hand takes something off his cheekbone, a fleck of something off a plate, and looks at it, and wipes it on his apron. “Gross,” she says, pleased with both of them, and goes back to her booth.
They leave together at ten. Margot caps all three pens, one after another. “Trial basis,” she says to Skye at the door. “If it’s boring they’ll kill it.”
“Then make me boring.”
“I’d lose my job.”
The plate in the corner booth has been eaten down to the purple. The fork is laid across it, and beside it on a napkin, in capitals, in Margot’s pen: *10. TELL GLORIA.*
When the booth is bussed he finds Gloria at the pie case, turning the boysenberry so its cut side faces the wall.

journal.title: Margot Lindqvist
journal.text: Margot Lindqvist. Has a folder on me. Called Lena and me useful idiots for Christian nationalism in front of four hundred people. Made a point about the Euthyphro I still can’t answer. Her mother teaches Classics at Reed. Held a wake for a cigarette on the roof and buried it at sea, for the prose. Had a brother. Her mother was forty-one; the test came back; they’d already picked the name. Anders. March 15, 2000. She’s defended her mother in every room since, and she defended her on the roof. Lena said his name. Doesn’t sleep. My friend. She has a faith column now, in the *Tide*, on a trial basis. If it’s boring they’ll kill it. She told me not to be boring. Came to Big Sur as an observer, for the monks — a functioning patriarchy in its natural habitat. Ran the *Tide*’s Ferrer follow-up from a minivan and wrote nothing down. Sunday at the coffee urn: ‘I’m not writing anything down.’ Halloween: Joan of Arc in duct tape, with her own haircut. Best Couple, with Pope Joan. She called it a category error and laughed anyway. Told me I’m surface acting. Hochschild, 1983. The flight attendants. On the stairs, about Julian: ‘He’s the healthiest thing in her life, Costigan.’ She meant it. Alarm Five: twenty-seven days; she’d said twenty-six. Out past one, four nights of six — she doesn’t sleep, she counts. Not writing it down. Sunday: UNEXPLAINED CITRUS. Nineteen on the solstice, four days early, under protest. Likes us. On the record. Lit a candle for research. Took Skye’s side about the rose. Goffman, 1956. Wrote TED in her notebook and underlined it. Gave to Partners In Health and sent the rest of us there — Farmer’s Catholic, sort of. Commented ‘Front stage.’ on my status. Wednesday night in the lounge, while Laney kept it short with Theo: keeping score. A page in her notebook says SKYE. Thursday at the Anchor she interviewed Skye for her column. She hated that it was good.

journal.title: Gloria (the Anchor)
journal.text: Hired me for rating her pie a four. Rated me a lattice-top. I’m not going to ask. Told her I won’t be the next guy at the door. She says nobody holds a door that long without somebody else walking through it. Asked after the pecan. I said she’s seeing somebody, he’s nice. She said lattice-top. Boxed a pie for Nonna. From a woman who’s been on her feet thirty years. Peach is August. St. Nicholas Eve, at the end of my shift, low, at the pass: ‘Pecan came to see if you were here.’ Gave my Thursday to Hector — his girl’s due at Christmas. ‘Don’t argue with a baby.’ Says I look like the pie case at closing. Rated somebody new. Boysenberry. ‘That one’s not waiting for any door.’ The last night: two forks and the pecan, at the counter. ‘That one’s still standing in it, hon.’ Thursday I asked her for Saturday night. ‘Who’s she?’ ‘You met her.’ ‘Boysenberry.’ She gave it to Rudy’s nephew.

choices.text: “I need Saturday night. It’s for her.”
choices.key: At the Anchor you asked Gloria for Saturday night off, and told her it was for Skye.
response: Gloria doesn’t turn around. “Who’s she?”
“You met her.”
Gloria turns the tin another quarter. “Boysenberry.” She raises her voice down the line without raising it much. “Rudy. Your sister’s boy still want hours?”
At the flat-top Rudy lifts the spatula over his shoulder without turning around. “*Mijo*.”
“Saturday’s his,” Gloria says. She shuts the pie case and wipes her prints off the glass with the hem of her apron. “Don’t make me sorry, hon. Bring her by for the peach in August.”

choices.text: “Family thing. Saturday.”
choices.key: At the Anchor you asked Gloria for Saturday night off. You told her it was a family thing. She knew.
response: “Your family’s in Ohio, hon.”
She lets him stand there with that, and goes on turning pies. “Who’s she?” she asks the glass.
He gives up. “You met her.”
“Boysenberry.” Down the line: “Rudy. That nephew still need hours?”
Rudy raises the spatula without looking round. “*Mijo*.”
“Saturday’s the nephew’s,” Gloria says. She hands him a rag for the pie case, since he’s standing there. “Tell your family hello, hon. All of them. Even the one with the Saab.”

choices.text: “Does the Anchor need me Saturday, or does it just like having me around?”
choices.key: At the Anchor you talked Gloria out of your Saturday night.
response: “It survived the Johnson administration,” Gloria says. “It’ll survive you.” She slides the pie case shut. “Who’s she?”
“You met her.”
“Boysenberry.” She doesn’t make it sound like anything. “Rudy. Your nephew.”
From the flat-top the spatula goes up over Rudy’s shoulder and comes down again. “*Mijo*.”

“There,” Gloria says. “Now the Anchor’s got somebody it likes having around.” She takes a napkin out of her apron pocket, the one that says *10. TELL GLORIA.*, and smooths it out on top of the pie case, and leaves it there.

s06.slug: FRIDAY · 4:50 PM · OCEAN ROAD, THE SAAB
body: The top is down, because it’s her car and those are the rules, and the sun is going into the water at the far end of Ocean Road slowly enough to watch it go. They’re parked on the bluff side with the engine off. He’s behind the wheel, where she’s had him all week to get used to it, and she’s in his flannel in the passenger seat with her feet up on the dash and her toes spread to catch the last of the warm.

At the twelve-ten today the Gospel was the four men who couldn’t get their friend through the crowd and took the roof apart over Jesus’ head to let him down. Jack has had the roof in his head all afternoon: the dust and the plaster coming down on everybody, and nobody stopping them.
“I’m going to bed at nine,” Skye says. “Tonight. Like a child.”
“It’s Friday.”

“Surf people are farmers.” She moves one foot off the dash and into his lap, as if it lives there. “I’m going to eat dinner at five-thirty like a retired dentist in Ventura and be asleep by nine with my light on, so Tomás knows I mean it. I’m picking you up in the dark. You’ll hate me. It’ll be very romantic.”
“Is Tomás coming?”
“His wetsuit is. In spirit, he’s coming.” She wiggles the foot in his lap. “Wear something you can get sand out of. There isn’t anything you can get sand out of. Wear something you don’t love.”

On the radio KCLU has come to the part of the hour where a woman reads the community calendar in a voice like warm milk — a pancake breakfast in Lompoc for Haiti, a second collection at the Mission on Sunday, a benefit concert tonight at eight at Café Bastille on Mission Street, every dollar to Catholic Relief Services — and Skye reaches over without moving her feet and turns it down.

She read the flyer on Wednesday. She was at the table when Theo asked Julian how many of the songs were about her, and Julian said *One*. She looks out at the water. The sun goes the rest of the way in, and the sky over it turns the color of the inside of a shell, and she lets the radio stay low.
Her foot is still in his lap. He puts his hand around her cold ankle, and she lets him keep it there, and wiggles her toes at the place the sun went, asking it for an encore.

choices.text: *Go to Julian’s benefit at Bastille tonight. It’s for Haiti.*
choices.key: Friday night you went to hear Julian play for Haiti at Bastille.
response: “I think I’m going to go to that,” he says. “The thing at the Bastille. It’s for Haiti.”
“Go,” Skye says. “It’s for Haiti. Six o’clock. I’ll honk.”
She takes her foot back out of his lap, gets out, and comes around the hood to take the wheel back, and on the way past she knocks twice on the hood with her knuckles, to tell the car it did fine.

choices.text: “Come to a movie with me. Opening night. It’s about my book.”
choices.key: Friday night you took Skye to *The Book of Eli* on opening night.
response: “You have a book?”
“*The* book.”
“Oh,” Skye says. “That one.” Her feet are already down off the dash. “Out. Switch. You stall when you’re excited, and I want popcorn before the previews.”

s07a.slug: FRIDAY · 8:00 PM · CAFÉ BASTILLE, MISSION STREET
body: Bastille at eight is string lights and the hiss of the steam wand, and every one of the mismatched chairs is taken by ten to. People stand two deep along the brick wall under the French posters, and the barista in the Che shirt has stopped steaming milk and is only making change. On the chalkboard by the register somebody has written SONGS FOR HAITI — EVERY DOLLAR TO CRS, and under it, in a different hand, *no requests*.

At the front table, by the stool and the mic stand, there’s a coffee can with a paper sleeve taped around it — CATHOLIC RELIEF SERVICES, in the purple marker from Tuesday night — and a clipboard, and Lena, in the gray cardigan, with her back to the room. She keeps it to the room all night. Jack stands by the door with his hands in his coat, and knows where it is anyway.

Laney has the chair beside her. There are jingle bells laced through the top eyelets of her boots, two to a boot, and they go every time she crosses her legs. “I said *bells*,” she tells Margot, who is writing. When Julian comes through the tables with the guitar case she catches his arm. “You are going to be *wonderful*, Julian. I can feel it in my boots.” She sees Jack over Julian’s shoulder, by the door, and turns back around to the stage.

Margot is on the bench along the wall with a reporter’s notebook. Kevin is beside her with a hot chocolate he bought so he’d have something to hold, and when Jack catches his eye he leans out from the end of the bench. “Question,” Kevin says, over the room. “What does a person wear to a sports bar? Asking for a girl with four brothers.” Margot, writing: “Armor.”

Theo has come and leaned on the door frame next to Jack in the navy blazer, with an espresso. “Pledge assignment,” he says. “Attend a cultural event and report on it to the brothers in fifty words or fewer.” He looks out over the room, the bells, the coffee can, the back of Lena’s head. “I’m going to need more words.” After that he doesn’t say much of anything, which on Theo looks like effort.

Julian has two friends with him: a girl from the music building on a borrowed upright bass and a boy sitting on a cajón. They start with songs everybody knows, and people sing the choruses back at them, badly, because it’s for Haiti and it doesn’t matter.

Between the second and the third Julian leans in to the mic. He doesn’t talk much on a stool; when he does it’s low and dry. “The can’s up front,” he says. “Lena has it. I’d put something in.” He tunes a string. “I’ve seen her with a clipboard.” The room laughs. At the front table Lena doesn’t turn around, but one hand comes up over her shoulder with the pen in it, and the room laughs again.

From the door Jack can see the back of her neck under the pencil in her hair, and the place where the cardigan collar folds over, and her shoulders, which are up. He has known that set of her shoulders since September. He has never once had to stand at the back of a room from it with his hands in his coat.
Before the third song Theo leans an inch toward Jack. “Is this the one?”
Jack doesn’t answer. It isn’t.

Before the fourth, Julian leans in to the mic. “I learned this one Tuesday night from a guy in my theory class,” he says. “His family’s in Port-au-Prince. He made me promise I’d say the words right. So I’m going to go slow.” And he does. It’s in Kreyòl, and he sings every word of it carefully and doesn’t make any kind of face about doing it, doesn’t perform the care; he only gets the words right, one after another. The room goes very still. At the front table Lena’s head goes down and stays down until it’s over.
“Is this the one?” Theo says, under the applause.
Jack lets him have that one too.

Halfway through, Laney gets up and goes to the counter for a water and comes back, and both ways she passes close enough to Jack that the bells go against his shin, and both ways she looks straight through him to the door.

Three more, one of them his own. Then Julian tunes for a long time with his head bent to the sound hole, and the bass player sits down on the edge of the stage to listen, and the boy gets off the cajón.
“This one’s new,” Julian says. “It’s called ‘First of the Year.’”

It starts on a river. Jack knows the river; he has never seen it. Julian picks a figure low on the strings that moves like slow water, wide and heavy, and over it there are barges anchored out in the middle of the current with the fireworks loaded on them, waiting, and a long cold walk along the top of the levee with the whole city counting backward behind it. A girl in a borrowed coat. The Moonwalk, he calls it, and the name of it is half the song.

Then midnight, in the song. The barges go up. And in the minute when the year turns she is looking down at her phone with the light of it on her face, and he doesn’t ask her who. That’s the chorus — *and I didn’t ask* — and the rest of it is what he did instead: he looked at the river, and he let her have the minute.

There’s a bridge where every boat on the river blows its horn at once, and Julian leaves a hole in the guitar for it, a bar of nothing, and in the hole you couldn’t have heard her if she’d said anything. In the song she doesn’t.
In his coat pocket Jack’s hand has found the RAZR. It closes on it. It doesn’t take it out.
Tuesday comes back to him in one piece: the flyers they folded side by side on the carpet in the Newman lounge, Julian’s folds straighter than his.

Lena doesn’t look at anybody. Not at the stage, not at the room; her eyes are on the clipboard in front of her, and the pen in her hand doesn’t move. Laney looks at Jack. Beside him, Theo has stopped asking.

The last chorus comes around, quieter, and Julian takes it down to almost nothing, and lets the river have the end. When he stops, the room holds a moment before anyone claps, and then everybody does, longer than a room this size usually has in it. Julian looks at the floor in front of the stool until it’s over, and then he plays one more, a loud one everybody knows, to get them out the door. Laney sings it louder than anyone in the room, standing, with the bells going.

Julian comes down off the stool and goes to the front table, and Lena stands up for him. He says something to her Jack can’t hear from the door, and she nods, and he puts his hand on the back of her neck, under the pencil, briefly, and lets go, and goes to pack up the guitar.
Theo has written on a napkin against the door frame. He shows it to Jack: *Nine songs, two originals, one in Kreyòl, bravely. Bells.* “Too long?” he says. “Brooks likes it lean.”

Out on Mission Street it’s cold and dry and the crowd comes apart slowly under the streetlight, saying goodnight in clumps. Lena is on the bench outside the window with the coffee can between her knees, counting it — the bills in stacks on her thigh, the coins in her palm — and Laney beside her holding the clipboard and the pen. Each time someone goes by, Lena looks up and thanks them, by name if she has it.

Theo goes past the bench and folds a bill into the can without breaking stride — a hundred; Jack sees the corner of it — and Lena says, “Thank you, Theo,” and Laney writes it on the clipboard without lifting her eyes to him, and Theo goes on up Mission Street with his hands in his pockets.
Kevin and Margot come out together. “I’m bringing her tomorrow,” Kevin tells Jack, going by. “To Sully’s. A person. I’m bringing a person.” He stops at the bench. “Great work, Lena.”
“Thank you, Kev,” Lena says.
Margot takes him by the elbow and steers him on toward the car.
“Eleven hundred and six,” Lena says to Laney, and Laney writes it down, and the bells on her boots go.
Jack is the next one going by. Lena looks up.
“Thank you for coming, Jack,” she says. “It’s for Haiti.”
It’s what she said to the couple in front of him.

choices.text: *Put a twenty in the can.*
response: He takes the twenty out of his wallet that was going to be the week, and folds it once, and puts it in the can.
Lena holds her hand out for the pen without looking, and Laney puts it in her hand, and she writes it on the clipboard herself. “Eleven twenty-six.” She hands the pen back. “Thank you.”
Down the block Julian is loading the bass into somebody’s hatchback. He waves with the case.

choices.text: *Nod. Say goodnight.*
response: He nods. “Goodnight.”
“Goodnight, Jack.” She goes back to the coins.
He doesn’t put anything in the can. He told himself on the way over that he would, and he doesn’t; it would be a thing done in front of her, for her to write down.
He gets to the corner before Laney stands up off the bench. He hears her bells behind him the length of the block.

choices.text: “It was good, Lena. The river one.”
response: “It was good, Lena,” he says. “The river one.”
Her hands stop on the stack.
“It was,” she says.
And she takes the bills up off her knee, all of them, and starts the count over from the top, though she had it right the first time. Laney looks at the clipboard and writes nothing.

s07b.slug: FRIDAY · 7:20 PM · THE RIALTO, MISSION STREET → 9:40 PM · THE SAAB, THE BLUFF ROAD
body: The Rialto is the last single screen on Mission Street: a marquee missing every fourth bulb, a woman in the ticket booth reading a paperback with her thumb in it, a lobby carpet patterned red and gold so it never has to admit to anything. Under the marquee Skye stops in front of the poster, Denzel with the sun behind him and a blade over his shoulder. “He carries a book across America,” she says, “and they gave him a sword for the poster. That’s marketing. That’s my industry in one sheet.” Opening night of *The Book of Eli* has filled the house about two-thirds, mostly men on their own and couples on early dates. She has the popcorn buttered in layers — “middle and top, I’m not an animal” — and folds herself into the seat beside him with her knees up and her feet on the armrest she has claimed for both of them.
Halfway through the previews her hand comes into the popcorn after his and finds his hand in there instead, and keeps it, buttered, for most of an hour.

On the screen the country has burned down to gray, and Denzel Washington walks west across it with a pack on his back, a machete, and a book he won’t let anybody touch. Skye doesn’t know the lines. She knows the man. Half a second before he says anything she leans in and whispers how he’s going to say it — *low* — *he’s going to wait* — *he’s going to be polite about it, so somebody dies* — and Denzel goes low, and waits so long that the man in front of them shifts in his seat, and is polite about it, and somebody dies. She’s right nearly every time.
“How,” Jack whispers.
“He’s Denzel. He always waits.”

The first time he catches her it’s an hour in, at night in the picture, the man reading from his book by a fire with nobody to hear it. It gets Jack under the ribs: thirty years of carrying one book and reading it out to the dark. He turns to say so and finds her face turned off the screen and lit by it, on him. She looks back at the screen. The second time, near the end, she doesn’t bother.

They’re up on the bluff road by twenty to ten, in the Saab with the top up, for once, because it’s January and she has lost an argument with it, and the windows have started to go. Her iPod is in the deck, low, something driving and electric she says is for the freeway and they aren’t on one. The platforms are lit out on the black water. They’ve been arguing since the lobby.

“He didn’t need the book,” Jack says. “That’s the movie. He had it by heart. That’s how it worked from the start — the Church was saying Mass for sixty years before anybody wrote a Gospel down. It lived in the people who carried it. The ink came after.”

“Then why did everybody kill each other over the copy?” She has her back against her door and her knees up. “You people burned a man for translating it. Tyndale. I looked it up in the lobby, on my phone, in the bathroom line, while you were being a gentleman about the napkins.”

“That was —” He stops. It was outside Brussels, and the man who argued hardest against him is a saint. “Thomas More wrote against him,” he says. “More’s a saint.” He looks at the fogged windshield. “I go back and forth on it.”
“Good,” Skye says. “Go back and forth on it. I like you when you’re losing.”

The blind business next. She guessed it, she tells him, in the first twenty minutes, and she counts the clues off on her fingers with enormous patience: he touches every wall he walks past; he hears everything before anybody else in the picture does; he turns his ear to a door instead of his face; “and *nobody* shaves that well at the end of the world with his eyes open.” He didn’t guess. He didn’t have the first idea until the lock came off and the pages were all bumps. She makes him say how many clues he missed. He says four. She says five — the sunglasses — and he says everybody in that movie wore sunglasses, and she says that’s what makes it a clue.

“Nobody should be the last of anything,” she says later, with the window behind her gone completely white. “It’s too much for one person. It makes you walk past people. He walks right past a woman getting dragged off the road, because the book comes first, and I’m supposed to think that’s holy.”
“The movie thinks it’s a sin. He says so, after.”

“*After*.” She pulls her sleeve down over her hand and wipes a hole in the fog the size of a coin, and looks at the platforms through it. “Everybody should carry it. Badly. In little bits. That’s the only safe way to carry anything.”
“That’s a parish,” Jack says.
“What is?”

“Everybody carrying it badly, in little bits. You just described St. Brigid’s. Sister Rose carried it into a room of thirty-one boys who’d rather have been anywhere else, with a whistle. The ushers carried it by counting the collection wrong for forty years.”
“Show me St. Brigid’s sometime,” Skye says. “And the sister with the whistle. I want to see what you look like scared.”

And then her Chesterton. Not his: the copy she bought used on Ventura without knowing whose book it was, and she’s further into it than he would have bet. “He says the madman isn’t the one who’s lost his reason,” she says. “He’s the one who’s lost everything except his reason. That’s the Gary Oldman guy. He had the only reasonable plan in the movie. Get the book, use the book, run every town in the West with it. It all made sense. He just didn’t have anything else.”
“That’s my book you’re quoting.”
“It’s my book. I paid four dollars for it. You have a different copy.”
“And it was in Braille the whole time,” he says. “Think about that. The one man who wanted it most finally gets it open and can’t use it. It was no good to anybody who only wanted to use it.”

“That’s a very good ending.”

“It’s a *Catholic* ending. The thing protects itself, and the man who carried it gets to die happy.” She points at him through her sleeve. “And then they print it. On Alcatraz. On a press. You said it didn’t need ink, and the last ten minutes of your movie are a man getting it back into ink as fast as he can.”

“Because people forget,” Skye says. “That’s what ink is for. You people talk like the book’s for the ones who already know it. It’s for the people after.”

Somewhere in there she does him as Denzel would play him. She drops her voice to the floor of the car and says *Tyndale*, very slowly, and then waits, and waits, with her eyes on his, until he cracks. “See?” she says. “Somebody always dies.”

The windshield is white from pillar to pillar, and the platforms are gone behind it. Her feet have found his thigh. She’s waiting, with her chin on her knees, for him to say something good enough to win.

s08.slug: SATURDAY · 6:10 AM · MARISOL POINT — THE INSIDE
body: She honks at ten to six, ten minutes early, two short taps that come back off the front of Delgado in the dark, and he’s already on the curb with his bag, because she warned him about farmers. The top is down. It’s January and it’s forty-some degrees and the top is down, and she has the iPod up loud on something with a pounding piano and two people shouting happily over it, much too happy for the hour, and she sings along with the parts that don’t have words. On Seacliff, with the cold coming over the windshield at them, she tells him why it’s worth it: the wind. Before the sun the air comes down off the land, or it doesn’t come at all, and the water lies down glassy and holds its shape. By ten the wind’s come around off the sea and chops everything to pieces. “Morning is when the ocean’s honest,” she says. “After that it’s just weather.”

She pulls into the dirt lot at the end of Seacliff at ten past six, past the last house, and kills the engine and the lights, and the dark comes down on them. There’s no moon. The stars go all the way down to the Channel, so many of them the sky looks dusty, and up on the bluff the lighthouse is a shape where the stars stop. Out past it, in the black, the Point is breaking: a long crack, then a roar that goes on a while, then nothing, then the crack.

They change by the dome light. Hers is a black suit with the knees worn shiny. His is Tomás’s old one, from tenth grade, she says, before Tomás got big, so on Jack it’s short in the arms and tight across the back, and his wrists stick out of the sleeves like a kid who grew over the summer. It’s still damp from whenever it was last worn, and getting into it is like being swallowed, slowly, by something cold that has its doubts about him. She zips him up the back with a knee in his spine. The board is the soft-top with the bite out of its rail.
At the edge of the water, before they go in, she says the first half of the Hail Mary under her breath, with his *thee* in it. “For the waves,” she says, when he looks at her.

They wait for grey on the cold sand. She sits between his knees on the soft-top with her back against his chest and his arms around the front of her suit, for warmth, she says, and names the stars for him, wrong, on purpose — that one’s Cleveland, that one’s Bob — until he corrects one, and after that she knows every one of them, and the year she learned them, for a planetarium voice-over she did at fourteen that nobody heard. Five shapes come down the path past them in the dark, men with short boards under their arms and nobody talking, and go into the water without stopping and paddle north toward the noise. He loses them before they’re past the shore break. For a while he can hear them out there, a word now and then coming back over the water.
“That’s the reef,” Skye says. She points at the noise. “We’re not going there.” She points south, at a quieter sound, a long hush and fizz. “We’re going there.”

The dark starts to come apart at twenty to seven. It goes from black to the gray of a chalkboard, and the water comes up out of it gray on gray: out at the Point the reef break standing up in long dark walls, with the five shapes sitting black on the swell beyond it, and south of it, close in, the sand bar, and the white water running in over the bar in low broken lines, over and over, somebody shaking out a sheet.
He is still very bad at it.

Most of his falls go the way December’s went. One goes worse. He gets his knees under him on the soft-top, and a foot, and the other foot, and for the space of a breath he’s up in the white water with his arms out, and the nose catches and the board leaves from under him as if somebody called it home, and he goes over the front of it into the wave. The white water takes him and rolls him the length of the bar. His shoulder hits sand. The cold gets into both ears at once and roars there, and everything is gray and loud and he has no idea which way is up, and then his knees find the bottom in two feet of water and he’s kneeling in the shallows with his hair in his eyes, coughing salt, with sand down the inside of Tomás’s suit to the small of his back, where it will stay for the rest of the day.
Skye paddles over and sits up on her board beside him, dripping, very interested.
“It feels the bottom and it trips,” she says. She points at him, kneeling on the sand bar. “You’re the bottom.”

On the eighth try or the ninth he stands up. Two seconds: the soft-top running straight in on the white water, and him on it, upright, arms out, knees bent the way she showed him, nobody’s idea of a surfer and standing. Twenty yards out Skye screams. It isn’t a word. It’s a scream, with both arms in the air, loud enough that one of the black shapes out at the Point turns its head. He’s in the water again a second later, and she’s still at it, and when he comes up she’s paddling at him as hard as she can to tell him what he looked like.
“A holy card,” she says, out of breath, slapping the water. “Arms out. Shocked. A guy on a holy card who just got told the thing.”

The sun comes up at five past seven behind the hills and gets to the top of the bluff before it gets anywhere near the water. From out past the white water, sitting on the boards with their legs hanging down into the cold, they can see it, what she drew on his half-sheet: the swell coming in straight from the open sea and bending as it crosses the reef, every line of it wrapping in toward the same rocks.
“Field data,” Skye says, and spits salt. “Write that down.”
“I don’t have a pencil.”
“Remember it, then. You’re the one with the memory.” Between sets she points up at the bluff with her chin.
Up there at the wall above them, in the first sun, there’s the white cross.
“Somebody leaves flowers up there every week,” she says. “They’re new on Sundays. Tomás says since spring.”
Jack looks up at it. He knows the name on the crossbar.
Her page has his name on it now.
Out past the reef a set is standing up. “Paddle,” Skye says, and he paddles.
Later, sitting out past the white water with the sun on their backs and his hands gone white, she tells him about six in the morning.

“Not one person has ever taken a picture of me at six in the morning,” Skye says. “Not on a set, not at a premiere, not a girl in a lecture hall. It’s the only hour I’ve got.” She runs her palm along the rail of her board. “The guys out at the Point don’t care who I am. They care if I drop in on them.”
“Do you?”

“Once. I was fifteen. A man named Gator told me what he thought of me in front of everybody, in words I’d never heard before, and he was right.” She watches the next line of swell come bending in around the reef. “I never did it again. Gator taught me more than the stunt double.”

They come out at eight, blue, his teeth going. On the sand at fourteen past, with the boards stuck nose-up behind them, she holds the white phone out at arm’s length with its back turned toward them, because there’s no other way to do it, and takes three without being able to see a thing, and looks at them, and keeps the second one. It’s the two of them in wetsuits with all of the morning behind them going gold, her cheek against his shoulder, and a stripe of wet sand down the side of his face from his eyebrow to his jaw that he didn’t know was there. She types with her thumb.

body: Sully’s on a playoff Saturday is black and gold from the green awning in. The shamrock in the window still has its one leaf out, and under it the place is packed to the walls with people who sound like Lena or like her cousins, standing three deep at the bar for a game that hasn’t started. The big screen at the back has the Superdome from the blimp. The five tube televisions up in the corners have it smaller, in five slightly different greens. Somebody has taped a fleur-de-lis cut out of a pizza box to the register.

One of the tubes, the one over the kitchen door, isn’t on the game. It’s on CNN with the sound off, because Lena asked the owner, and by now he says yes to her about everything. Port-au-Prince from a helicopter: the airport with its one runway and a gray cargo plane sitting on it, more planes up in the haze waiting their turn, pallets of water shrink-wrapped on the tarmac in the sun and going nowhere. A man on a street holds a plastic jug up to the camera, upside down, to show it’s empty. The picture goes back to the helicopter. For the rest of the afternoon it’s there at the edge of Jack’s eye, over the kitchen door, whichever way he turns.

Two tables have been pushed together end to end under the brass ship’s bell, a long table with a head and a foot. At the head, under the bell, in her Brees jersey, Lena has the rope laid across both palms with the frayed end hanging over her wrist. Julian is beside her in a gray cardigan with a borrowed Brees jersey pulled on over it, a size too big, the number hanging off him. Laney is on her other side. Down the long sides: Margot, who is here, she has told everyone, for the anthropology; Kevin, and beside Kevin a girl in a 49ers cap; Joey Abruzzo, who is nineteen tomorrow and has told everyone that too. At the end of the bar, level with the foot of the table, one stool stands empty with a folded Sully’s napkin on the seat.

Skye comes in at Jack’s side in a black sweater and a gold scarf she bought at the Rite Aid on the way — “This is as far as I go,” she told him in the car — and Theo comes in behind them in the navy blazer, straight from a pledge breakfast, with Hollis riding in his teacup. Up at the head of the table Lena sees them. She leans to Laney and says something short. Jack can’t hear it over the pregame. Laney nods.
Then Lena ties the rope off to the cleat on the post and comes down the long side of the table to meet them.
“Skye,” she says. “Welcome.”
“Lena.”
“Thank you for the thank-you,” Skye says.
“It was Newman’s.”

“Y’all take the foot. It’s got the big screen straight on.” Lena pulls the corner chair out herself and sets it facing the screen, and then points at the stool by the bar. “Don’t sit in Dale’s chair. He’s had it since September.”
She says all of it at an ordinary volume, with her hand on the back of the chair, and there isn’t a thing wrong with any of it. Jack would rather she’d thrown the bell at him.
“Skye, this is Julian.”
Julian stands up to shake hands. It’s a handshake you could leave your car keys with.
“The flyers,” Skye says.
“The flyers,” Julian says, pleased.

body: “Loved the one about the river, Julian,” Theo says.
“Thanks, Theo.” Julian takes it as a compliment, and on him it turns into one.
Laney hasn’t gotten up. Skye goes up the table to her anyway, with something closed in her fist, and sets it down by Laney’s root beer: two little jingle bells on a pink ribbon.
“You said with bells on.”

Laney looks at the ribbon. Then she lifts one boot onto the rung of Julian’s chair, and the bells laced through her top eyelets go. “I wore my own.” She puts the ribbon in her purse, not on the table, and snaps the purse. “Word to the wise, since you brought a present. Let him win the arguments. He likes to feel tall.”
“I’ve seen your work, Price,” Jack says.

Something at the corner of Laney’s mouth starts toward the old grin and comes back. She turns to Julian. “Sugar, scoot.” Julian scoots. “Theodore, you’re over there with your friend.” She points the root beer down the table, at the foot.
Theo goes where he’s pointed. Jack takes the end chair, Skye the corner on his left, Theo the corner on his right, across from her.

Margot lifts her glass to Skye down the length of the table — subject to author — and Skye lifts hers back. Before the kickoff Skye has asked Clare about the violin, how long and who taught her and what she plays at the 11:30, and has talked to Kevin about nothing in particular — the fries, the parking, whether San Jose counts as the Bay — easily, keeping him company, until his shoulders come down from around his ears.

On Arizona’s first play from scrimmage a Cardinals running back finds a seam on the left side and is gone, most of the length of the field with nobody near him, and Sully’s goes so quiet Jack can hear the fryer.
Skye is on her feet. “He ran so *far*!”
A hundred Louisianans turn around and look at her.
“Wrong team, kid,” says a voice at her elbow. Dale has come in at the kickoff, Barry Sanders jersey and all, and he’s standing by his stool with a root beer, and he says it gently.

By the end of the Saints’ first drive Dale and Joey are teaching her the chant, one on each side of her, Joey at full Staten Island and Dale under his breath — *Who dat* — and she gets it wrong three new ways and then right, and does it at the big screen with both fists, and the next table over turns around and does it back at her.

When the Saints punt she cheers that too, because it went so high. Dale explains punting to her, patiently, as a form of giving up. She says it’s the saddest thing in sports. Dale says she hasn’t met the Lions.

Between plays she adopts Dale. Jack watches it happen. She asks where Warren is, and Dale says Michigan, not the other one, and she asks what he did there, and he says Warren Truck, twenty-seven years on the line, Dodge Rams. Instead of saying *oh*, she asks him what the line sounds like at shift change.
Dale thinks about it. “Like church letting out,” he says. “Everybody talking at once.”
“And the first Monday after?”
Dale lifts his chin at the screen and watches the Saints line up. “Got up at a quarter to five,” he says. “Habit.” He drinks his root beer, and that’s the answer.
Jack knows that chin. He has eaten breakfast across from it.
Joey climbs onto the rung of his chair with his root beer in the air. “Tomorrow I’m nineteen,” he tells Sully’s, “and in eight years I’m a priest!”
The next table cheers. Somebody at the bar yells *Father Joey*.
“Can priests watch football?” Skye asks him.
“Father Osei says it’s the only time he prays in Twi.”

Halfway down the table Clare is explaining the nickel to Kevin. “Five defensive backs. They take a linebacker off. It’s third and long, they want speed.” She has four brothers in San Jose; she mentions them like a varsity letter. Kevin nods, and tells her about concussions — the brain moving inside the skull, the cumulative effect, a study out of Boston — through two plays and part of a third, and Clare listens to every word of it with her cap pushed back and asks him a good question at the end.

The Saints answer. Brees takes them the length of the field in a handful of plays, and they score, and at the head of the table Lena is up under the bell with the rope unhitched and in both hands, and the brass goes over and back and shouts, and the bar shouts with it. Jack watches the bell. Skye watches Lena: both hands on the rope, ringing one pull past where anybody would stop, and one more, with her eyes on the screen. Skye watches it to the last pull. Then she turns back to Dale and asks him whether Lions fans have a chant.
Late in the first quarter the Saints have the ball, third-and-four, and Arizona calls time out, and Joey crosses himself.
Skye sees it. “Wait. Is that *allowed*?”
“Is what allowed?” says Joey.
“Praying for a first down.” She turns in her chair. “Is it? You’d know. Is God allowed to care about third-and-four?”
“It’s allowed,” Jack says. “It’s just not how it works. He’s not a vending machine. You don’t put in a Hail Mary and get a first down.”

“Why not?” She points her root beer at him. “Your Chesterton. Chapter four. Grown-ups get bored, so they decide God must be bored, so they decide the sun comes up because it has to. And he says maybe it’s the other way. Maybe God’s like a little kid who says *Do it again* to the sun every morning. Maybe He makes every daisy separately and never gets tired of it.” The bottle swings to the big screen. “A God who makes every daisy separately can care about third-and-four.”
Up the table Julian laughs, surprised into it.
“Chesterton was talking about the sun,” Jack says. “Not the Cardinals.”
“You pray for parking.”
“St. Anthony’s for lost things. Parking is a lost thing.”
“Two thousand years slower, you said.” She leans in across the corner of the table. “Third down is *right now*.”

“She’s *right*, Jack!” Joey tells the bar. Margot has turned her chair all the way around to face the foot of the table and is following every exchange with her head, deadpan, delighted. Kevin has gone quiet over his plate of fries.
From his stool, without taking his eyes off the screen, Dale says, “My Lions prayed. Didn’t take.”

They go at it hard and laughing, Skye up on one knee on her chair, Jack with his elbows on the table, and the timeout runs long for a truck commercial, and the table has stopped pretending to watch the truck.
At the head of the table Lena has the rope across her knees, and her hands have gone still on it. She is watching the truck commercial on the big screen as though there will be a quiz on it.

Jack’s eyes go up the table to the head of it, to the girl under the bell.
Skye sees them go. She turns her head and looks where he’s looking, and then at the big screen.

On third-and-four Brees drops back and throws, and the ball comes down in the end zone in somebody’s hands, and the bar goes up all at once, and Lena is up with the rope, and the brass shouts over all of them, and nobody is arguing about anything anymore.

choices.text: “Fine. He cares about third-and-four. He just doesn’t owe us the first down.”
response: “Fine,” Jack says. “He cares about third-and-four. He just doesn’t owe us the first down.”

“Cares, doesn’t owe.” Skye points at him. “Somebody put that on a holy card.” And she’s winning, so she keeps swinging. “And if He cares about third-and-four, look where you are.” The bottle takes in the room: the table, the bar three deep, the bell. “These people’s city went under the water. Four years of novenas and candles and a football team on its back. You think He looked at all that and said, *Sorry, I don’t do sports*?”
Jack’s eyes go to the head of the table. Lena is under the bell with the rope across her knees.
Skye watches his eyes go. She follows them up the table, and then puts her own back on the game.

The Saints come out of the timeout and Brees converts it and then some — into the end zone — and the place stands up roaring, and Lena is on her feet with the rope in both hands, and the bell takes the argument away from all of them.

body.text: He watches the rest of the half from Dale’s end of the bar, with Skye on the stool beside him chanting it correctly now, and Dale buying the root beer, and the long table forty feet away under the bell.
body.else: The rest of the half goes by at the table. The Saints pull away and keep going, never in doubt by the half; Lena rings the bell when there’s cause; and the foot of the table is quiet in a way the head of it isn’t.

body.text: Somewhere in the second quarter Theo comes up to the bar for a refill he doesn’t want and stands at Jack’s elbow with Hollis in his teacup, and says it low, while Skye is turned away teaching Dale the breath: “She’s the best actress I know, Costigan. Never ask her if she’s acting.” Then he takes his root beer back to the table. It’s short, for Theo. When Theo lies he furnishes it, down to the drapes; when he means a thing it comes out small. Jack can’t tell which way this one cuts, toward her or toward him.

Never ask her if she’s acting.” Then he straightens a cuff and looks at the screen. It’s short, for Theo. When Theo lies he furnishes it, down to the drapes; when he means a thing it comes out small.
