body: At halftime he gets up and goes back toward the restrooms. To get there he has to pass the head of the table. Lena’s chair is empty, her jacket on the back of it. Julian is at that end by himself, reading the label on her root beer, and he lifts it at Jack as he goes by: decent, friendly, nothing in it, a man at a game he doesn’t follow enjoying it for somebody else.

The back hall at Sully’s is narrow enough to touch both walls: the men’s and the women’s, a mop bucket with the mop standing up in it, the kitchen’s swinging door with its round window gone yellow, and by the fire exit a pay phone with its directory on a chain and half the pages torn out. Through the paneling the halftime music has come on out in the bar, loud enough to feel in the wall, and the long table is stamping along to it.

Lena is at the far end by the fire exit, in the Brees jersey, with her phone to one ear and a finger in the other. He hears her before she sees him. “No, Daddy, you can’t call Luc, Luc’s working, he’s got a radio, he knows the score. Give the phone to Mama. Daddy —”
“Daddy, breathe,” she’s saying. “It’s halftime. Breathe. I know. I *know*. I saw it. Go get some water and breathe.”

She sees Jack. She takes the phone down from her ear with her father still in it — a big man’s voice gone tiny in her hand, saying *did you see that, cher, did you see* — and the phone shuts on him, and it’s only the music through the wall.
“Did you tell Laney to do that?” It comes out louder than the hall needs. He hasn’t come down from the table yet; he can feel it still in his hands.
“Laney’s Laney.”
“She said one word to me all week, Lena. *Night.* Today she’s got a speech.”
“She said it to *me*.” Lena’s chin comes up. “At my table. She’s allowed to be on my side.”
“Your side of what?”
She doesn’t answer that. “You yelled at her in front of forty people from Louisiana, Jack. Over a joke.”
“It wasn’t a joke.”
“It was Laney. Everything’s a little bit a joke.” She folds her arms over the jersey. “She’s been my best friend since August. You don’t get to stand up in my bar and take her head off.”
“You said the Fishbowl.”
“I changed my mind.” She says it easily, the way you’d say you changed your mind about the soup.
“Why?”
“You don’t watch a playoff game in a dorm, Jack.” Her hand goes to the medal at the neck of the jersey and holds it.

The kitchen door bangs open and a waiter comes through sideways with a tray of wings up over his head, and the hall isn’t wide enough for three. Jack goes back against the pay phone and she goes back against the women’s door, and for as long as the tray takes to pass they are closer than either of them means to be. He can smell the beer somebody spilled down her sleeve in the first quarter. The tray goes by. They both step back farther than they need to, and she smooths the front of the jersey where the tray nearly was, as if it had touched her.
“Mrs. Fitch says hi,” Lena says, as if they were done, as if this were the mailboxes. “The lemon bars sold out.”
He doesn’t take it. “Skye was being nice to her. She brought her *bells*.”
“Skye was fine.” It comes quick, and flat. “She was halfway through her line when you stepped on it. It was a good performance.”
It’s out before she can stop it. He watches her hear it, a half-second after he does.
“Performance.”
“I didn’t mean —”
“You meant it.”
“She’s an actress, Jack.” There’s nothing light in it anywhere; she isn’t trying to be funny, and she isn’t. “I’m not being ugly. It’s her job to be good in a room. She’s good in a room.”
“She’s real.”
“I didn’t say she wasn’t.”
“You said performance.”

“I said she’s good at it.” Her voice comes up to meet his, and the music through the wall covers both of them. “Everybody at that table was watching a show today, Jack. You were in it. You were *good* in it.”
“So I’m fake too.”
“I didn’t say that either.”
“Then what are you saying?”

She looks at him a long second. Whatever she’s saying, she doesn’t say it. It gets as far as her mouth; he can see it there, and he can see her decide. And there’s one in him too, about a phone call on a Friday night and which one of them told the other to go on and have a life. It stays where it is. They stand there in a hall where you can touch both walls, with a whole sentence apiece and neither one of them spends it.

Through the wall the table roars at something — the halftime show, a replay, Joey — and she looks toward the noise, and back, and he sees how tired she is. It’s in her eyes. The rest of her has been perfect since one-fifteen.
“Atlanta,” she says. “I kept your chair till the half.”
And before it has finished being said she takes it back, with procedure. “Laney’s purse has it now. It’s a good chair.”
There’s an answer to that. It isn’t one a man can give in the back hall of Sully’s with the halftime show coming through the wall, and he stands there without it.

A big man in a Vilma jersey shoulders through from the bar toward the men’s room, sees the two of them, and says “Who dat” to them both, as a greeting. “Who dat,” Lena says back, warm, perfect, and he goes in happy.
She looks past Jack’s shoulder at the clock over the kitchen door.
“It’s ten after three.”

journal.title: The medal
journal.text: Lena’s medal was her grandmother’s; it came back to her mother in a plastic bag. When she’s working something out, her hand goes to it. At the Point in December. Thursday at Hale’s table, about Justine. Saturday in the hall at Sully’s, about the Fishbowl.

journal.title: Lena Broussard
journal.text: New Orleans. Two seventeen. Classics. Hale paired us for the semester. Makes a roux like she’s taking a vow and expects you to keep up. Her father sells Gulf shrimp — Broussard’s Seafood, Banks Street. Boyfriend: Wes Arceneaux — Tulane, civil engineering, the boat at sixteen. Calls at 8:04 on the dot. Her grandmother, Lucille Guidry, died in the storm in ’05; they buried her in November, in the good dress. The medal came back to her mother in a plastic bag. She has never asked her mother one question. The year after, she went to Mass every morning to yell at God, and somewhere in there it stopped being a fight. Paints a mean fleur-de-lis. Said hi to Danny. Says she’s going to be defense. Walked her home the long way from Pi Lam: the beach, the creek, the tower, the Commons, the Lagoon bench. Wes calls from somewhere loud lately; her brother Luc is with him. She’s decided not to notice. The Tuesday of the wake he called on the dot, from his room. He came for Columbus Day weekend to see the Pacific. She’d told him it’s a threat. He touched it at two in the morning. Came to Marisol for the money, she says — Notre Dame gave her half. Went to Hale’s office to tell him he was wrong about who gets to forgive. Cried for Anders on the roof and didn’t give an inch. Stayed till the chimes. There’s a sentence she hasn’t finished. Her middle name is Thérèse; October first is her feast. She erased *Show Lena* out of the Hopkins herself, so Danny could have it. At midnight I gave her *Story of a Soul* with my margins in it, and she wouldn’t let me erase a word. On the beach she asked if I know what I’m doing. I don’t. She laughed. At the elevator: ‘That was a terrible thing to be glad about.’ Brought Wes to everything. Wouldn’t walk past the last house on Seacliff toward the Point; said she was cold. At the stove she gave Becca the spoon. Monday night, two floors down, on the phone to New Orleans: ‘He’s my friend, Wes.’ Plays the piano in the Delgado basement — the one nobody admits to playing. Two years at the Rosary. At five in the morning she played the Saints on the Ferrer carillon with her fists, one bell flat, and said it wasn’t flat, it was New Orleans. Wes told her what I said on the beach, and what I didn’t. On a motel porch above Lucia at three in the morning she told me I can’t say her name like that. She asked what I decided. Not to be the one who wrecks anything, I said. She said okay. Then: me neither. Bought her Mémère a fruitcake from the monks, in exact change. ‘A girl writes the thing she wants first, Youngstown.’ Halloween: Flannery O’Connor, with a stuffed peacock tagged 57. Andalusia. She wouldn’t go past the last house on Seacliff, not even for Laney. ‘I came as her. I never said she was right.’ In the last minute of the extra hour, she put my hat back on. All Souls: she wrote her grandmother’s name in the book, and Nora Calloway’s. Nora was her host at Preview Weekend, in April. That night Wes ended it, on the phone, on the east stairs. He stopped going to Mass in September. There’s a ring. She knew something in September and decided not to notice — she says she’s good at it. At six in the morning she asked me what I’m going to do. She wrote Hale twelve pages in the spring of ’08, two years after the year she yelled at God. She’s had the same postcard the whole time. She knew mine on the porch. She had a house picked out on Zimple Street. A fig tree. She’d picked the paint. Veterans Day, on the bench above Campus Point: St. Martin gave the beggar half his cloak; she says everybody forgets the beggar took it. No. 9 for the reliquary. Friday the 13th, under the eucalyptus, in the middle of a sentence about monarchs: Julian asked her to dinner. So. Thursday night in the basement she played the piano properly — around the dead F. The last time she played it right in front of anybody was a November, four years ago. If you play well, she says, people ask you to play. Reading *New Moon* out of spite. Friday she signed the Manhattan Declaration from bed, with a cold. Two soups. She ate Julian’s. Mine’s on the sill for tomorrow. Ate Gloria’s soup cold out of the quart, at the sill, at six in the morning. Argued YES: a promise is made to a person, not to a reason. Wrote on my paper that I don’t believe one sentence of it. Neither does she. Mémère is lighting a candle for Nonna — the whole name. Half a name is half a candle. At the airport: Our Lady of Prompt Succor, for Nonna. She works fast. Thanksgiving: Theo said *pop* to the whole Broussard table. She asked about Theo, and Nonna, and her saint. Julian called during grace. Wes was in the kitchen. ‘Go back to your family, Youngstown.’ Handed Julian the bell rope at Sully’s. Knows I don’t work Mondays. Texted at two in the morning about Yusuf’s mother. On the lawn at four, looking at the place I wasn’t. Came to the Anchor at the end of my shift in Kevin’s car — Julian’s in Oakland, his brother’s home from the Navy. She has a paper. St. Nicholas Eve: Walgreens at half past one. I told her about Ma’s two hundred shoes; she said then we’re doing it, and we did every door in Delgado. Says I hold my phone like a hand of cards. Asked where I go. I said sometime. She said okay. Book Nine, for her Greek final: *Outis*. Nobody. In the laundry room she stepped back first. ‘Don’t make me be the one who wrecks something.’ Julian’s writing something she can’t hear yet. Twelve and oh in overtime. Her free hand found Kevin. Knows Book Nine by heart; asked me to pray at eight. Picked my best argument at the Brick: what a man says yes to. Put her phone face up next to mine and said nothing. Heard Julian’s song before anybody. ‘It’s good, Jack. It’s really good.’ Told me not to leave in the second chorus. The Advent party: I kept the whole room between us all night. She brought coffee to the white elephant, and I got it. Stole my 8-Ball. Won an argument about ‘Joy to the World’ with Isaac Watts. Didn’t play. Julian did. Friday night, half past twelve, she knocked on 412; Theo said the library. At the Mañanitas she told me about Juan Diego, who took the long way around the hill. Thirteen and oh. She texted me the number. After the Gaudete Mass she asked the 8-Ball something. Better not tell you now. Geminids from the roof without me. At Hale’s oral she’d answered him in Augustine — said my sentence was his. She defended it and won, and told him to ask where I say yes at two in the morning. Julian kissed her goodbye at his car; he’s going to New Orleans for New Year’s. Friday she knocked with two coffees and a list of every place. She played the basement piano for me, properly. Taught me a secret in the O Antiphons. Pecan at Gloria’s counter; fourteen and oh is ordained. On the Lighthouse porch she said it plain: I’d never not answered her before. Never missed Sully’s. Always came to her, whatever it was — and now I stay away. She knows something’s hurting. She didn’t make me say what. Walked past the last house to the Point for the first time all semester. The bonfires on the levee on Christmas Eve — call her from the garage. On the roof I nearly said it. The 8-Ball said ask again later. She gave me the tin to keep. I gave her Benedict. At the checkpoint she turned around and said something I couldn’t hear. Christmas week: her sister had the baby in the third quarter of the Dallas game, while they were still undefeated, so Beau didn’t get a vote. Lucille Odile — both grandmothers. Lena’s the godmother. Then they lost. The 8-Ball said very doubtful. She texts me the O Antiphons at dusk. Monday night she called at ten to one to argue about Pius, and won the point fair. I told her I’ve been sleeping in Danny’s bed. She said somebody ought to. When the Pope went down she texted within the minute: is he alright, are you. Christmas Eve she held the phone up to a bonfire on the levee so I could hear it burn. After Midnight Mass she wrote from the steps of Holy Rosary: an hour behind me, like she said. She’d mailed me *The Moviegoer* before the last night. Christmas night she told me how Réveillon went, and about the place her mother sets for her grandmother. Then she said her mama worked at Memorial. Nothing else. Holy Family: they lost to Tampa in overtime — ‘They’re resting.’ Fr. Dom took the short form; hers read the long one, and we’re not discussing it. Sunday night we whispered for two hours because Nonna was asleep in her chair, and she whispered too, from her back steps. I read her her own margins; she argued with the girl who wrote them. I told her Dad went in. ‘And Danny drank it.’ Julian calls at ten his time. Tuesday she called from behind the register at her father’s market — home field; her father’s making the musician a gumbo. I told her what Danny asked about the third. If Pop won’t get out of the truck, she says, I get in. She said she wouldn’t call as much. Then she said she’d call. Wednesday nothing. Thursday at dawn, the morning after Julian landed, she called from the river with beignets. She said she’d call. She asked if I asked Ma who the candle was for. No. You don’t. New Year’s Eve she texted at my midnight, an hour early for her. At hers it came the second the year turned — before the fireworks. I know what that means. Then the river on fire, and Julian beside it. New Year’s Day I called her from the garage at the half, and she said, You called *me*. Saturday night she called the house — Ma answered and talked to her for ten minutes. Two hours on the kitchen phone, her mother’s cordless dying twice. Her grandmother made the christening gown for Luc in 1985; it rode out the storm in Mémère’s cedar chest in Breaux Bridge. She had me be the priest so she could practice the promises. She thinks Binx doesn’t stop looking — he stops looking by himself. I told her Danny asked me something I can’t answer yet; she didn’t ask what. She asked how California was. ‘Come back, Youngstown.’ Two hours, and she never said Julian’s name. Lucille was baptized in the third quarter, and she didn’t get one word wrong. After that I called every night. Twelfth Night she got the baby in the king cake. Friday she said she hasn’t been fair to Julian, and she’s going to fix it. Sunday she landed: come find me tomorrow. Monday I couldn’t find her — not at 217, not at the twelve-ten. She came into Hale’s seminar a step behind him with a king cake, and the only chair left was next to mine. She was polite to me for fifteen minutes. Then Dido. Tuesday morning Julian put up a picture from their dinner Monday — birthday dinner, two days late. She’s tagged. She’d said call me after. I didn’t. At the mailboxes she asked about my break, and I told her as far as Denver, and Ma’s words about the coffee. ‘Tell her I’m glad.’ The baptism was lovely. Tuesday night at St. Brendan’s she had the whole thing organized by half past eight, in a whisper, and put me on the table with Becca. When the TV said trapped she left the room. Julian went. Wednesday at the table she met Skye. She said no pictures at the table, and I argued with her about it in front of everybody. That night at the desk: Skye’s envelope was the biggest. ‘Tell her thank you. From Newman.’ Thursday she took the far end of Hale’s table before anybody got there. Saturday she moved the Saints to Sully’s; she said she changed her mind. In the back hall she stood up for Laney, and said Skye gave a good performance, and wouldn’t say what she meant. At Atlanta she kept my chair till the half. At ten after three she told me the time.

journal.title: Theo Vance
journal.text: Roommate. Drives his grandfather’s car like a getaway. His father calls him Teddy and stays six minutes. Heard my brother’s voice and didn’t ask. Loves *Point Break* with no irony at all. Poppy texts him at midnight. The Big Sur Expedition, on his father’s letterhead. Called the Anchor and got my Saturday covered before I could say I work Saturdays. Bought six used copies of Kerouac off the cart at Driftwood. Halloween: threw the party of the year as Gatsby. Left it at twelve-thirty by the back gate. Found him at the wall at the Point at one in the morning, the second one. He said not there. Nineteen. His father sent a stretch Lincoln and a card that called him Teddy, and called at six minutes past and stayed four. His mother came up from La Cañada with Poppy. Blew out nineteen candles in one breath. Sunday night, to the ceiling: Laney says he asked if he could ask. ‘Like a vampire. They have to be invited in.’ He’s known since Friday. Wednesday I said I ended it. He opened his jar and gave me a spoon. Friday he took me to a party in Montecito so I wouldn’t meet anybody, and lost me in three minutes. Saturday at six he was on his bed in his coat. He’d called me nine times. At halftime of Michigan I asked him home for Thanksgiving. He said yes before I finished, and bought two tickets to Pittsburgh. ‘Guests bring something.’ Looked up St. Elizabeth’s visiting hours before I asked. Thanksgiving: came to Youngstown in Dad’s Browns parka over the camel coat. Dad said that’s not a coat. Speaks Italian from a movie, wrong. Rolled Nonna’s crust and made his own peach pie. Dad asked him to say grace. He did. Nonna asked who prays for him; he said nobody. Met Danny — Danny liked him in a minute. Didn’t talk the whole way home. Kept Rosie’s prince. Nonna gave him a twenty. Back at Marisol he reads me the News Feed in the morning like the intentions at the twelve-ten. Wants to know if I *like* things now. Says I’m fast. Says I’ve started sleeping with my phone. Played the Fishbowl a voicemail off the internet and ran one sentence of it twice: take your name off your phone. Timed my pocket with his stopwatch. Didn’t say the number. Taped Rosie’s princes over his desk; Nonna’s twenty is in the frame of his mirror. Covered for me at Alarm Five: I was in the shower. Sat on a dryer with Laney, discussing finals. Sunday at twenty to seven: back from somewhere. I asked him home for Christmas; so did Pop, in the garage. He has things in LA. ‘Tell your father I heard him.’ Put his cashmere on me Sunday. Said I was holding my phone like a rosary. Lent me the Burberry in the storm. Tried to heckle Julian’s song and couldn’t. Watched me go through Bastille’s window. Six in the morning on the last day of classes he asked why I look like I’ve been through a war. He had a question in his calendar for after Thanksgiving; he’s moved it. Sunday he filmed his shoes with a girl named Soledad. Tore up the tab. Left me his cashmere for Ohio. Have a good Christmas, Costigan — all of it. Christmas: called from LA to ask for Christmas Eve and Christmas Day. I answered on the first ring; he sounded surprised. Dad said he doesn’t have to call first. Wore the parka again. Ma glued his name on a stocking. Nonna has his cashmere. Ate an eel. Took my phone out of Rosie’s hand at dinner and gave it to me face-down. Christmas Eve he came with me to Trumbull, bought from the machines, and did Dad for Danny. Danny asked him who comes to see him. He said I do. Danny says he’s on the list for good. Wears the Browns hat now. Laney has a schedule. Landed in the middle of the night — they wanded the baccalà in Pittsburgh. At the side door Christmas afternoon he said, Be careful, Costigan. Of what. All of it. New Year’s Eve, at nine his time, the party was already a disappointment. Wore Ma’s scarf in sixty-one degrees. A woman asked if he was in a band. Back from LA in the orange hat and Ma’s scarf. Says the hat is a family heirloom. Sunday night: ‘Congratulations, Costigan.’ ‘Go to sleep. Monday is going to be a long day.’ Tuesday morning he did the responses too: Lord, hear our prayer. Rushing Sigma Rho; ate a raw onion in front of the lacrosse team. Wednesday night he got a bid. A pledge now. Carries a raw egg named Hollis in a teacup; if it breaks, he’s out. At Sully’s: ‘She’s the best actress I know, Costigan. Never ask her if she’s acting.’

response: “I’m sorry I missed Atlanta.”
She looks at him then, straight.
“It was a good game,” she says. Under the music she takes a breath. “Go on. He keeps the light on.”
She goes past him up the hall, and the door to the bar opens on all the noise of the place and shuts on it again behind her.
He stands by the pay phone a minute after, with the halftime show coming through the wall.

choices.text: “You moved it so I wouldn’t come.”
choices.key: In the back hall at Sully’s you told Lena she’d moved the game so you wouldn’t come. ‘You came.’
response: “You moved it so I wouldn’t come.”
“You came.” Her hand comes down off the medal. “Go on, Jack. He keeps the light on.”
She goes back up the hall sideways past him, and doesn’t touch him doing it, which in a hall that size takes some work. The bar door swings behind her twice and settles.
He stands by the pay phone with the halftime show coming through the wall and his hands open at his sides.

choices.text: *Say nothing.*
choices.key: In the back hall at Sully’s you said nothing, and Lena sent you to confession by the clock.
response: He says nothing. She waits long enough to be sure of it.
“Then go on. He keeps the light on.”
The waiter comes back through the kitchen door with the empty tray under his arm, and when he’s past, so is she.
The clock over the kitchen door says eleven after.

choices.text: “Keep the chair. I’ll stand.”
choices.key: In the back hall at Sully’s you told Lena to keep the chair. You’d stand.
response: “Keep the chair,” he says. “I’ll stand.”
Almost a smile. It gets as far as one corner of her mouth, and she kills it there.
“Then go on. He keeps the light on.”
She’s up the hall before the next song starts through the wall. Her jacket will be on the back of her chair, and Julian will be keeping it, and the bell will be where she left it.

s09b.slug: SATURDAY · 2:12 PM · SULLY’S, THE LONG TABLE
body: The extra point is good, and the broadcast goes to commercial, and the last of the bell is still up in the rafters with the neon. Skye stands and pats her pockets. “I need reinforcements,” she says, and goes up to the bar for root beers. Julian’s phone goes in his cardigan; he looks at it and says, “Oakland,” to Lena, and takes it out the front door. Through the window Jack can see his back on the sidewalk under the awning, the phone at his ear, one hand pushed up into his hair.

Up at the taps Skye has the bartender laughing inside of a minute. A girl in a Reggie Bush jersey leans over from the next stool and asks her something, and Skye says, “Only on Thursdays,” and the girl shrieks and grabs her friend, and Skye signs a Sully’s coaster for her with the bartender’s pen and slides a dollar into the tip jar on top of it. From the foot of the table Jack watches her lean on the bar on her elbows, the gold scarf coming undone, one boot heel hooked on the brass rail, saying something to the bartender that makes him put both hands over his face. Half of him is simply glad: glad of her, of the noise she makes in a room, of the fact that she’s here, in this one, on a Saturday. Laney is watching her too, the whole way to the taps and back down the bar again, with her chin on the heel of her hand.

At the head of the table Lena has turned in her chair toward the tube over the kitchen door. The helicopter again, the runway again, a line of people along a wall with buckets. She watches it with the rope across her lap and her thumbs on the knot at the end of it.

It’s the dead minute after a score, when a bar this full goes as quiet as it ever goes: ice, the fryer, a chair. Laney doesn’t lower her voice. She has never in her life lowered her voice. She leans back and says it to Lena.
“Oh my God. He found a California you. Excuse me while I go be a bitch on your behalf.”

It reaches the foot of the table without trying. At the head of it Lena’s hand stays where it is on the bell rope, and she doesn’t look down the table, and Skye comes back from the bar with two root beers sweating in her fists.

Laney waits until she’s sitting. “Loved your picture this morning,” she says down the table, sweet as tea. “So candid. Kenzie Rourke had it on her phone before I’d had my coffee. Who does your candids?”

“My arm,” Skye says, and holds the arm up and turns it in the light, like something she won at a fair. Joey laughs, and the girl in the 49ers cap laughs, and Skye lets them, easy, the way she let Corinne talk on Wednesday until Corinne had talked herself out. Jack can feel her deciding how the rest of it is going to go. She’s already decided. She’s good at this.
“And is he a series regular,” Laney says, “or more of a guest arc?”

Under the table Skye’s hand finds Jack’s knee and grips it, hard enough to hurt. He can feel each of her fingers separately, and the nails through his jeans. Above the table she is smiling with every tooth she owns, and nothing about her shoulders has moved at all.
“Series regular,” she says. “They picked up the —”

She doesn’t get to the back nine. It comes up the back of Jack’s neck before he knows what it is — heat, under his collar, into his ears, the place on his knee where her fingers dug in singing with it. He has been a lot of things with Laney Price since August. Scared of her. Bossed by her. Saved in his phone because she put herself there. Never this. All week he has looked up tables and down hallways for the reason, and found Julian’s arm along the back of Lena’s chair, and two girls at that end gone cold on him for something neither of them will name, and he has taken it, because he didn’t know what he was taking. He knows what this is. This one isn’t at him.

His chair goes back on the boards. His voice comes out over hers, over the fryer and the ice and the dead minute after a score, louder than he has ever been in this bar, louder than he knew he had in him.

journal.title: Laney Price
journal.text: Laney Price. Pi Lam, as of Thursday: ran back across Seacliff in a pink cowboy hat to Lena first. The night before, on the floor of 217 in a white dress, she asked what happens if they look at her and see. First Catholic Mass: arms crossed like a Baptist, came back from the blessing pink and quiet. Programmed herself into my phone. (Hoodie status: hers.) Pi Lam’s barn party: carried upstairs by her new sisters, glorious and wrecked. Called Lena a mother over the banister. Said sorry at the sign of peace, at her second Mass. Big/Little: Sloane is her big. On the front steps at one in the morning, in a PI LAM LITTLE shirt, with a balloon on her wrist, she told me about Kaylee Whitmore. Fifteen; Kaylee drove; they’d both been drinking and Laney let her. Preston Road. A culvert. A cast for six weeks that everybody signed. A month later, a doctor’s note for flying; she’d never been on a plane. Lena’s the only other one who knows. In the water at Pfeiffer Beach she caught my swan. It’s Theo’s. Her fourth Mass, up a mountain with the monks. Asked Lena how you light a candle, and lit one. Don’t you dare, she said. Halloween: Pope Joan, in a cardboard mitre with gold rickrack. Blessed Del Playa from the widow’s walk until Rafi’s father asked her to come down. Over a bullhorn. Best Couple, with Margot. Went missing with three pledges for most of the extra hour; Kevin found her at Lupe’s with a burrito. She’s not stupid. She’s hungry. Friday at the Situation Room: ‘Who’s that?’ ‘No one.’ Alarm Five: ‘Fireman. You’re dressed.’ Saturday on the laundry table with Theo and a legal pad, discussing finals. Somebody put an orange in her Ugg. She’s crying. The Advent party: black velvet, in mourning for Advent. A Texas thing in the punch; Kevin took her flask. Asleep on the porch swing by a quarter to eleven. The ninth at nine at the Anchor, with an agenda on an index card: pie, no questions. Sunday night she came out of my room with her laptop and went past me without a word. Since Sunday she hasn’t said a word to me. At the Haiti table she met Skye, and gave a hundred dollars to the clipboard. Wednesday night in the lounge she was keeping it short with Theo, for a nod. Then, to me, without turning her head: ‘Night.’ At Sully’s Skye brought her a present. She wore her own bells. She gave Skye advice, and I told her I’ve seen her work. Then she took a shot at Skye, and Skye was handling it, and I didn’t let her. I’ve never yelled at Laney before. The whole bar heard.

choices.text: *Straight at her, full volume:* “She’s not a guest, Laney.”
choices.key: At Sully’s, when Laney took her shot at Skye, you didn’t let Skye finish. You told Laney, loud enough for the bar, that Skye isn’t a guest.
response: “She’s not a guest, Laney.” The next table turns around. He doesn’t care. “She’s not an arc. She’s not a season. She’s not anybody’s candid. She’s here because I asked her, and she brought you a present, and you’ve had all week to say whatever this is to my face. You said one word. *Night.* So say it to me. Not to her. Me.”

Kevin opens his mouth — “Respectfully —” — and Clare, without seeming to do anything, puts her hand on his sleeve, and he shuts it again. Joey is looking hard at his fries. Margot’s pen has stopped. At the head of the table the bell rope gives one small jerk in Lena’s hands, and settles, and she keeps her eyes on the screen.
Under the table Skye’s grip on his knee lets go. Her hand stays, and her thumb goes back and forth across the place where the nails were.
Laney is looking at him. Not at Skye; at him, all of him, the whole length of the table, as if he were a word she’d been spelling wrong since August. For once in her life she has nothing to say.

choices.text: *On your feet. Every word slow, and loud enough to carry.*
choices.key: At Sully’s, when Laney took her shot at Skye, you didn’t let Skye finish. You stood up and took Laney apart, slowly, for the whole bar to hear.
response: He stands. He doesn’t shout it; he doesn’t have to. He says it every word set down by itself, like something heavy he doesn’t mean to drop, and it goes to the end of the bar and back.

“You don’t get to do that. You’ve had six days to say it to me, and you said *Night*, and you saved the rest for somebody who walked in here with bells for you in her fist. That’s not being on anybody’s behalf, Laney. That’s just mean, and you’re better than mean. I’ve seen you be better than mean.”

Nobody at the long table moves. Kevin starts a “Respectfully —” and Clare’s hand on his sleeve finishes it for him. At the head of the table Lena’s thumbs have stopped on the knot of the rope. Jack sits back down. Under the table he puts his hand over Skye’s on his knee, and her fingers turn over under his and lace in and hold on.
When he looks up the table again, Laney is already looking at him. She doesn’t look away, and she doesn’t answer, and her chin has come up off the heel of her hand.

choices.text: “A note from the writers’ room, Laney: nobody ordered the spin-off.”
choices.key: At Sully’s, when Laney took her shot at Skye, you didn’t let Skye finish. You went after Laney loud and funny and mean, and then turned the table over to Dale.
response: “A note from the writers’ room, Laney.” It isn’t a joke voice. It’s loud and it’s furious and the jokes are just what the fury happens to be made of today. “Nobody ordered the spin-off. *Bitter Sorority Girl Takes Shots at Strangers.* One season. Canceled. You want to review somebody, review me. I’m the one who brought her.”
The next table over has turned around. Joey says “Oh, no,” very quietly, to his fries. At the head of the table Lena has gone so still on the rope that the frayed end has stopped swinging.
He isn’t done; he’s just done with Laney. He turns in his chair. “Dale,” he says, still too loud. “Tell them what she asked you about the line.”

Dale turns around on his stool with the nickel half explained. He looks down the table at all of them. “She asked about shift change,” he says. “Twenty-seven years. Nobody in California ever asked me about shift change.” And he turns back to the bar.
The table looks at Skye a little differently after that. Margot does, anyway; she moves her chair a quarter turn toward the foot of the table and leaves it there. Skye has gone pink to the scarf.
Laney doesn’t look at Skye at all. She’s looking at Jack, at what’s still on his face after the jokes, and the jokes haven’t gotten any of it off.

choices.text: *All of it, with the whole bar listening. Then take her up to the bar.*
choices.key: At Sully’s, when Laney took her shot at Skye, you didn’t let Skye finish. You gave Laney all of it in front of the whole bar, then took Skye up to Dale’s end in the middle of a drive.
response: “What is *wrong* with you?” Loud enough that the bartender turns the music down without being asked. “Six days, Laney. Six days you walk past me like I’m furniture, and the first whole sentence you’ve got is for *her*? She brought you a present. She came to *your* bar, for *your* team, in a scarf from the Rite Aid. You want to be a bitch on somebody’s behalf, do it on mine. Do it to me. I’m right here. I’ve been right here all week.”
Every head at the long table is down except two. At the head of it Lena’s hands have gone white on the rope.

“Come on,” he says to Skye, and the chair scrapes again, and Kevin jumps. “I’ll teach you the Who Dat properly.” He takes her hand and her root beer and walks her up to Dale’s end of the bar in the middle of a Saints drive, down the length of the long table, in front of everybody, which nobody in this bar does in the middle of a drive. At the bar he turns her around by the shoulders to face the screen and teaches her the chant right — where you take the breath, which word you lean on — and Dale beats time on the bar with his knuckles, and doesn’t ask.
From there he can see the table. Laney isn’t watching the drive. She has her root beer halfway to her mouth, and she’s watching him over it, and she sets it down without drinking.

s10.slug: SATURDAY · 3:11 PM · SULLY'S → MISSION STREET, THE SAAB

body.text: At Dale’s end of the bar he bends to Skye’s ear and tells her, and her keys are out of her jacket before he’s finished. Theo has drifted up from the table again and is standing at Dale’s other elbow, explaining the egg. “Go,” Theo says. “I’ll watch her.” Down the long table Laney’s face turns on Theo, slow and entire. Under the bell Lena has the rope in her hand again and doesn’t look up. Jack goes back to the foot of the table for his bag.

Theo, in the chair beside hers, looks up from the halftime show. “Go,” Theo says. “I’ll watch her.” Across the table Laney’s face turns on Theo, slow and entire. Under the bell Lena has the rope in her hand again and doesn’t look up. Jack gets his bag out from under the chair.

body: On Mission Street the top is down and Skye drives with both hands on the wheel, under the limit, past the Saturday traffic and a man selling Saints flags out of a shopping cart, and Mission Street has started honking for the score. She has the chant now, most of it, and at the light by the bank she does it at the man with the cart, and he does it back, and she drives on through the green like a woman just elected.
“For the record,” she says, with her eyes on the road, “I had it handled.”
“I know you did.”

“I had a whole thing. The back nine was the setup. There was a callback. It was going to *kill*.” She checks the rearview like a girl taking her driving test. “And at the risk of losing my feminist card, which I worked very hard for —” she signals for a lane change nobody else on Mission Street is using, and makes it at fourteen miles an hour — “that was kind of hot.”
He looks at her. She keeps her eyes on the road.

body.text: “*Nobody ordered the spin-off.*” She bites her lip on it. “I’m stealing that. I’m going to say it to Corinne.”
“You stood *up*.” She bites her lip on it. “Slowly. Like a sheriff.”
“*She’s not a guest, Laney.*” She does him, a half-octave down, and bites her lip on it. “At full volume. In front of the Who Dat people.”
“The bartender turned the *music* down.” She bites her lip on it. “Nobody’s ever made a bartender turn the music down for me.”

body: “Don’t do it again,” she says. Then: “Do it again. I’m going to reward that sort of behavior, Jack. Definitely. I want that on the record too.”
“It’s Saturday,” she says. “It’s three-thirty.”
“Ten after.”
“Then I’m speeding.”
The needle is on twenty-two.
Mission Street goes by. She lets a block of it go by before she asks.
“So.” She doesn’t look over. “You went to the bathroom at halftime for nine minutes and came back looking like the mop won.”

He could give her nothing. He has given her nothing about Lena for a month; it’s the one door in him he’s kept shut, and she has never once tried the handle. He doesn’t know why today is different. Maybe because he’s still angry enough to be stupid. Maybe because she had his knee in her fist under the table and never let her face move.
“Lena was back there,” he says.
Skye nods at the road. Her hands stay at ten and two.

“We were close. In the fall.” He hears how small the word is for it and leaves it. “Really close. She was — we were friends. We were good all the way through break. And then I got back, and it’s this. Her. Laney. Like I did something.” He looks out at the Saturday traffic. “I don’t know what I did.”
That’s all. It’s all true, and it isn’t all of it, and it’s more than he has said out loud to anyone.

Skye doesn’t say anything for half a block. She is listening to the part he didn’t say; he can see her doing it, the way she listens to a director give a note, her whole face turned toward something just past the windshield. He doesn’t know what she hears.
“Really close,” she says, trying it, the way she tries a line to see where the weight goes.
“Yeah.”

“Okay.” A breath. “So when we were fighting about third down, and she watched a truck commercial like it owed her money —” She stops herself. She puts the blinker on for Ocean Road, carefully, the most law-abiding turn ever made in Marisol. “Never mind. I’m going to be extremely mature about this. I’m going to hate her a very tiny amount, privately, as a hobby. Like needlepoint.”
She says it bright, and it’s a joke, and it’s nearly all a joke. Her thumb is going back and forth on the wheel, one small steady stroke, and she doesn’t seem to know it’s doing it.

“Thank you for telling me,” she says. “You don’t have to tell me the rest. I can tell there’s a rest.” And then, before it can sit there: “You were right to yell at Laney, though. I want that on the record also. The record is getting very long.”

And there it is, on Ocean Road, at twenty-two miles an hour. He told her a true thing about Lena, the first one, and she took it, and didn’t make him pay for it, and handed it back lighter than he gave it to her. In a visiting room in Trumbull with the vending machines going, Danny asked him one thing: *Which one of ’em can you tell the truth to?* He didn’t have an answer then. He thinks he has one now. She’s driving.
She pulls in at the curb in front of St. Brendan’s and leaves the engine running.
She leans over the wheel to look up at the A-frame through the windshield, the steep roof coming nearly to the ground on both sides. “It’s smaller than I pictured.”
“Am I still famous in there?”
“Nobody’s famous in there.”
“Then what do you tell him?”
“I tell him about me.”
Skye looks out through the windshield a long time at what there is to look at, which is the parish lot, and the olive tree over the courtyard wall, and the door. She looks at the door.

She wants to know. Not what he did; what he *says*, in there, to Him. She has wanted to know since December. On her porch Wednesday night she said *amen* after him and meant it, and that same day she was in Becca’s apron at a card table taking twenties for Port-au-Prince, and nobody asked her to do any of it. Christmas night in Youngstown Nonna looked up from her beads at the phone lit in his hand and said *Due ragazze*, and then: *Quale ti fa pregare?* He didn’t answer her. He doesn’t answer her now, out loud. But a girl who sits outside a church on a Saturday afternoon wanting to know what he tells God — he thinks that might be enough. He thinks it might be the whole answer. He believes it, sitting there, with the engine running.

The white phone lights in the cupholder. She reads it and laughs, and reads it to him. “Ted. *I have your seat. The redhead is drinking a cranberry juice at you, with a lime. It is a cosmopolitan in spirit.*” She turns the phone face down on her knee. “I’m going back.”
“You don’t have to.”
“Somebody should see the end of it for you.” She pushes her sunglasses up into her hair. “And I’m not letting the redhead have the second half.”
She leans across the gearshift and kisses him, short, a curb kiss with the engine running, and sits back. He gets out with his bag and stands in the open door.

choices.text: “Save me a seat.”
response: “I’m saving you Dale,” Skye says.
She leans across the empty seat and pulls his door shut herself, and swings the Saab around in the middle of Ocean Road, and heads back toward Mission with one hand up over the windshield for him.

choices.text: “Don’t let Dale teach you the second verse.”
response: “There’s a second verse?”
“No.”
“Then I’ll write one.” She reaches across and pulls his door shut on him herself, and U-turns on Ocean Road with the radio coming up, already singing something that isn’t the Who Dat yet.

choices.text: *Kiss her back, longer than she started it.*
response: He leans back in through the open door and kisses her again, longer than she started it, his hand along her jaw, until somebody behind them on Ocean Road taps a horn and goes around.

She’s laughing when he lets her go. She reaches across the seat and pulls his door shut herself, and turns the Saab around in the road, and it’s gone down Ocean Road toward the game with her hand up over the windshield.

s10a.slug: SATURDAY · 3:20 PM · ST. BRENDAN THE NAVIGATOR, THE FRONT STEPS
body: Ten minutes. He sits on the top step of St. Brendan’s with his bag beside him and the A-frame going up behind his back, all that blue glass dark from the outside on a bright afternoon. Ocean Road is Saturday-quiet. Somebody across the street is washing a truck with the radio on, and the radio has the game, and he doesn’t listen to it.
What he has in his ears isn’t the bar or the bell. It’s *It’s ten after three*, in her voice, and *He keeps the light on*.
In the side pocket of the bag, his own pack, as it rode home, the zipper shut on it since Wednesday night. In the front pocket, the tin. Eleven, her count.
The lighter is in his coat. He has it out without having decided to, and he’s turning the wheel with his thumb, not hard enough to strike.

choices.text: *Light one. Your own.*
response: He takes one of his own out of the pack and lights it with his back to the doors. On the steps of a church, ten minutes before confession. He smokes it halfway and doesn’t taste it, and grinds it out on the bottom step, and puts the end in his pocket so it won’t be on Father’s steps in the morning.
Then he picks up the bag and pulls the church door by its iron ring.

choices.text: *Put it back.*
response: He puts the lighter back in his coat and keeps his hand off it. Across the street the man shuts the hose off and stands back from his truck to look at it, dripping, as if it might have changed.
At twenty-eight past he picks up the bag. The door has an iron ring for a handle, cold from the shade, and he pulls it.

choices.text: *Open the tin. Count them.*
response: He opens the tin on his knee and counts them with one finger.
Eleven.
He shuts it and puts it back in the front pocket and runs the zipper closed, and gets up, and pulls the door by its iron ring.

s11.slug: SATURDAY · 3:30 PM · ST. BRENDAN’S — THE CONFESSIONAL
body: Inside, the afternoon comes through the blue glass on the west side and lays the pews out in long blue bars, and up where the two slopes of the roof meet it’s already evening. At the back, by the doors, the coat closet: the index card turned out, KNOCK (gently), and over the frame the little light is on.

Mrs. Fitch has her card table set up beside it, as she does every Saturday, with her lanyard and her ledger and a Folgers can with CATHOLIC RELIEF SERVICES taped around it in her own printing. She sees him look at the bare end of the table. “Lemon bars are Sunday,” she says, and goes back to her pencil.

Two folding chairs along the wall are taken. On one, a woman from town with a canvas market bag on her knees and the green tops of leeks sticking out of it. On the other, still in his Saints jersey, Joey Abruzzo, who left Sully’s at the two-minute warning and beat Jack here on the bus. “Birthday eve,” Joey tells him, in what for Joey is a whisper and for anybody else would be a toast. “Clean slate for nineteen. I’ve got a ride back for the third quarter.”
The closet door opens on an old man with a cane, who nods to everybody on his way to the sun, and Joey knocks and disappears inside.

The door is the door they hung in 1962, and Joey is Joey. There are no words in what comes through it — Jack makes sure of that, and so does Mrs. Fitch, who starts humming *Holy God, We Praise Thy Name* at her ledger at a volume she has been setting since the Carter administration, and keeps it up through every verse, and on the second verse the woman with the leeks comes in under her without looking up. When the door opens again Joey comes out red to the ears, dips his whole hand in the font, crosses himself twice, and heads up the side aisle for the Marian shrine. The woman goes in. When she comes out she sits back down beside a man in a windbreaker who has just come in from the lot jingling his keys, who must be her husband, and who looks like he’s been parking the car since three.
Jack knocks, gently, and steps in, and takes the kneeler.

The closet is the closet: the linen screen on its frame with the violet of the stole behind it, the old hooks along the back wall, the Prodigal Son on the inside of the door. On the far side the chair takes the priest’s weight, and the leg goes where it goes.
“Bless me, Father, for I have sinned. It’s been two weeks since my last confession. At home.”
“Jack,” Osei says. Only that.
On the steps he had a list. In here he keeps it to what will fit through the screen.

“At home I told Father Dom about the phone. All of it. That’s done.” He looks at the coat hook nearest his head, which has a drip of the wall’s paint on it from some year when nobody bothered to take it down. “The week after New Year’s she sent me a picture. At my parents’ house. I kept it, and I wrote back.”
“Monday night. Her room.” The words for it are short ones, and he has them, and he uses the fewest he can. “It went further than it’s ever gone. I stopped. I stopped at the last —”
The sentence stops where he did. He lets it.
“It’s the same every time. It goes a little further, and I stop a little later, and I come in here.” And then the thing he walked in carrying, which isn’t a sin yet. “I’m seeing her tonight.”
Osei is quiet. Out past the door Mrs. Fitch turns a page of her ledger, and the husband coughs, and the 11 goes by on Ocean Road with its brakes squealing at the corner, and Osei is still quiet.
“In December,” he says at last, “I told you that you were not avoiding the occasion. You were scheduling it.” The chair gives a little as he moves the leg. “Now you have scheduled *me*.”
Jack opens his mouth, and there isn’t anything in it. He thinks of the Saab doing twenty-two down Mission Street so he’d make it, and a clock over a kitchen door. It’s true. He had help.

“You came at half past three because you will be with her tonight,” Osei says, “and you would like to go to her with nothing on your account.” There’s no heat in it at all. “There is an old name for counting on mercy to cover what you have already decided. Presumption. It is a sin against hope, my friend — not against her. Against hope. Hope asks God for the strength. Presumption asks him for the receipt.”
Behind the linen the shadow of his head bends, and comes up.

“This morning’s Gospel. The physician comes for the sick, not the well. Good — come sick, and I will open this door every time. But I was a doctor a long while, and a doctor who stitches the same cut every Saturday is allowed to ask what you are doing with the knife.” A breath. “I am not your permission. I will be here every Saturday you come; I would much rather that than you stopped coming. But one of these Saturdays you will bring me the thing you cannot take back, and you will have decided it at half past three, in this closet.”
Out in the church the woman’s husband shifts on his folding chair, and the chair creaks.

“You told me in December that you want her good. I believed you. I still do.” Osei’s voice is lower now, and nearer the screen. “Then it is her good you are deciding at half past three as well, and not only yours.”
And then the question, with no proverb on it.
“Do you want to stop?”

choices.text: “Not tonight. I want to want to.”
choices.key: At confession you told Father Osei the truth: not tonight. You want to want to.
response: “Not tonight,” Jack says. “I want to want to.”
Outside the door the husband’s keys go into a pocket and come out again.

“That is the smallest beginning there is,” Osei says. “God takes less. He has taken less from me.” The chair creaks. “A man who wants to want is standing at the door with his hand on it. I have watched men come the whole way in from there. Bring me that, if that is what you have. But bring it before, not after. Before, it is still a prayer.”

choices.text: “Yes. I don’t know how.”
choices.key: At confession you told Father Osei yes — you want to stop — and that you don’t know how.
response: “Yes,” Jack says. “I don’t know how.”

“Then don’t go to her room tonight,” Osei says. “Sit on her porch. Sit in her car with the light on. Take her somewhere with a waiter who interrupts. In Kumasi we say a man who will not move his chair complains all night about the draft.” Through the linen, something that might be a smile. “I am not telling you to leave her, my friend. I am telling you to move the chair.”

choices.text: “I’ll stop before it gets there.”
choices.key: At confession you told Father Osei you’d stop before it got there.
response: “I’ll stop before it gets there.”
“You told me that in December,” Osei says. “Twice.” A pause through the screen. “I believed you both times. That is my sin, not yours.”

The leg shifts on the chair. “Stopping is a grace, and I thank God for every one. But you have just told me where you stopped on Monday. A man who keeps walking out to the edge to prove he can stop there is not practicing stopping. He is practicing the edge.”

body: The 11 takes Mission Street at a Saturday crawl and stops at every corner whether anybody wants it to or not. The driver has the game on a transistor radio rubber-banded to the fare box, the Saints up by four touchdowns and the announcer already talking about next week. Across the aisle a woman sits with a laundry bag between her feet, reading a *TV Guide*. Jack sits with his temple near the window and says it under his breath to the glass: the Our Father, and then the Hail Marys, ten, counted off on his fingers against his knee, and each time he comes to *pray for us sinners* he puts her name in where the *us* goes. *Skye.* The woman turns a page. He says the Glory Be and starts over for himself, with his own name, and he’s on the eighth when the green awning goes by the window and he pulls the cord and finishes it on the sidewalk.

The game has been over since the third quarter. The Superdome on the big screen is a party with two minutes of football still to play in it — forty-five to fourteen — and Sully’s hasn’t sat down since the punt return. He stops in the doorway, under the shamrock, and not a soul in the place turns around.

The long table is on its feet. Joey is on his chair. The Saints kneel on it, and kneel on it again, and the clock runs, and the bar counts the last ten seconds down in one voice the way they do in Times Square, and at the gun Lena has the rope in both hands under the bell.
She turns, and holds it out down the table. To Skye.
“Our guest,” she says.

Skye looks at the rope, and takes it, and rings that bell like the building is on fire. The brass goes over and back and over, and the table comes in under it with the chant — *Who dat, who dat* — and Laney is looking at Lena, not at the bell, and Dale at the end of the bar has put his root beer down to applaud with both big hands, and Theo is standing at the foot of the table, clapping slowly, his face beautifully arranged.

Lena sees him first. Her hand is still out where the rope was, open and empty, and over Skye’s shoulder she finds him in the doorway; the hand comes down, and closes, and she reaches past Julian for her jacket on the back of the chair.
Skye sees him a heartbeat later. She holds the rope up at him over everybody’s heads like a prizefighter’s belt and rings the bell one more time, just for him, and the owner lets her.

Out on the sidewalk Mission Street is honking. A pickup goes by with a fleur-de-lis bedsheet tied across the tailgate and three boys in the back yelling the chant at the stoplights. The sun is going down behind the hills, and the sky over the wharf is still light. Skye walks backward ahead of him to tell it, the gold scarf coming loose.

“Dale bought me a root beer. With *quarters*.” She drops into Michigan, flat as a parking lot, chin up at an invisible screen: “*Kid’s a natural.*” And back. “He said that. To the bartender. Not even to me. Joey says I’m going to be a Catholic by the Super Bowl, and I said I’m a Saints fan now, isn’t that most of it, and Joey had to sit down, and Ted said Joey should be a bishop.” She stops walking backward and just walks, beside him, her arm through his. “The redhead smiled once. Ted has witnesses.”
“Once?”

“Once. In the fourth quarter. At Dale.” She tips her head onto his shoulder for half a block. “Kevin explained what a concussion is to me. Twice. Clare held my hand under the table for the second one. Joey wrote the chant on a coaster in case I forget it overnight.” She pulls the coaster out of her back pocket to prove it: WHO DAT, in ballpoint capitals, and under it a phone number with a 718 area code. “That’s his mom’s. In case of emergency. And then at the end they gave me the bell.”
She stops on the sidewalk outside a dry cleaner’s and turns him around by the arm to face her, and she’s lit up from the inside like a jukebox.
“Jack. That’s the best thing anybody’s ever handed me in a bar.”

A car honks at them, for the Saints, and she kisses him on Mission Street anyway, and somebody leaning out the passenger window yells *who dat*, and she yells it back without quite taking her mouth off his.

They eat burgers on the hood of the Saab in the lot behind the wharf while the flags go by out on Mission, and then she drives the coast road north with the windows down and nowhere to be until the last light is off the water. By the time she turns onto Del Playa it’s nearly ten, and down at the Las Olas end of Seacliff Lupe’s white truck is just pulling in to put its lights up.

s11b.slug: SATURDAY · 4:05 PM · ST. BRENDAN’S, THE SIXTH PEW
body: Through the side windows he hears the 11 come to the corner and sigh and go on without him.

He’s in the sixth pew on the Lady’s side, on the kneeler, with nothing in his hands. The church is empty but for the votives at the shrine, Joey’s new one among them, and a man asleep in the last pew with his shoes off and set side by side on the kneeler beside him, toes to the aisle, as neat as a pair in a store window.
He has no beads. He has ten fingers and the back of the pew in front of him.
“For Skye,” he says, low, to the front of the church.

The Our Father. Then the Hail Mary, the whole of it — *Hail Mary, full of grace, the Lord is with thee* — through to *the hour of our death*, and before each of the next ones the same two words, said to the same place: *For Skye.* A Hail Mary is a Hail Mary. He doesn’t add to it. On the fourth the man in the back turns over and says something to his shoes. On the eighth a car goes by on Ocean Road with somebody leaning out of it shouting the chant at the A-frame, and he keeps going under it. Ten, on his fingers against the wood. The Glory Be.
Then the second decade, for himself, by the name he was baptized with, which turns out to be harder to say in an empty church than hers.

At a quarter to five the light over the closet door goes off. Osei comes out with the violet stole over his arm, genuflects to the tabernacle with the leg taking the long way down and the long way up, and goes up the side aisle to the sacristy, past the sixth pew, without turning his head. Jack is grateful to him for that past anything he could put into words.

The RAZR has been going in his pocket since a quarter past four, on silent, buzzing against the wood of the kneeler like a trapped bee, and he hasn’t looked. He opens it now, in the pew, and reads them in order, and they keep coming while he reads.

body: He sits back in the pew with the phone open on his knee, and the man in the back is awake now and putting his shoes on, one and then the other, slowly, as if there were a right order. On his way out he stops at the end of the sixth pew, a gray man in a Raiders cap who smells of the bus.
“They win?”
“Forty-five to fourteen.”
The man thinks about it. “Good for them people,” he says, and genuflects with a hand on the pew end, and is gone up the aisle into the light.

The Saab comes around the corner onto Ocean Road at ten past five with the top down and a little paper Saints flag somebody gave her stuck in the windshield frame, and she’s telling him the second half before he has the door open: Dale’s quarters, the chant all the way through, Joey nearly in tears at the end, everything, in order and then out of order. They eat at Lupe’s truck on Seacliff, sitting on the hood, with horns still going for the Saints all the way down to the beach, and drive the coast road with the heater on and the top still down because she refuses to put it up on a night like this, and it’s close to ten when she turns onto Del Playa.

s11c.slug: SATURDAY · 3:49 PM · ST. BRENDAN’S — THE CONFESSIONAL, THEN THE NAVE
body: He says the Act of Contrition. He has been saying it since he was seven, and it goes the way it always goes until the last line, *and to avoid the near occasion of sin*, which he has said a thousand times and never before with the occasion already on somebody’s calendar, in pen.
Behind the linen the shadow of Osei’s hand comes up.
“…and I absolve you from your sins, in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.”
“Amen.”
“For your penance —” Osei stops. “In December I gave you a decade for her, by her name, and you had the name and I didn’t. What is her name?”
He hasn’t said it in this closet. “Skye.”

“Skye,” Osei says, carefully, setting it down where he can find it again. In that voice, unhurried, it sounds like a name off a parish register. “A decade for Skye. By her name. Not ‘a girl,’ not ‘her.’ Before God, not before me. And one for you, by yours.” The chair takes the leg’s weight. “I will say one for her myself tonight. Now I can.”
“The Lord has freed you from your sins. Go in peace.”
“Thanks be to God.”
“One more thing.” The chair, the leg. “Next Saturday. Whatever you bring.”

He comes out into the blue. The husband in the windbreaker is on his feet with his keys in his fist, and the light over the closet door stays on for him. Mrs. Fitch slides the Folgers can along the card table toward him; he puts in the five he has, and she makes a mark in the ledger.

Up at the Marian shrine Joey has a taper and is taking a long time over which red cup in the rack is the lucky one. He chooses, and lights it, and kneels, and he’s still on his knees when a horn goes twice on Ocean Road. Joey jams the taper in the sand, genuflects at a run, and is out the side door into the courtyard with the jersey flying.

The clock over the choir loft says four minutes to four. The 11 stops at the corner of Ocean and Mission at five past and goes back down Mission Street past the green awning, where it’s still the third quarter, going on the fourth. The pews in front of him are empty all the way to the altar rail.
Ten Hail Marys for Skye, and ten for him. They’re owed either way.
