s12.slug: SATURDAY · 10:00 PM · DEL PLAYA, HER ROOM
body: The lamp is on. It sits on the floor by the mattress under its paper shade and makes one warm circle on the blankets, and past the circle the room is January: the bare boards, Sol’s boombox with nothing in it tonight, and over the bed the black window, the one that was in a picture once, with no stars in it. The cloud came in after sunset. The house is theirs. Skye bought Sol off with her parking spot through February, and Tomás is at somebody’s Saints party on Trigo and has sworn on his board not to come home at all.

body.text: She kicks the bedroom door shut behind them with her heel. “The second half was better with you in the doorway,” she says, and takes the Carhartt off his shoulders and throws it at the chair, and misses.
She kicks the bedroom door shut behind them with her heel. “You missed the bell.”
“You told me.”
“I told you *in capitals*.” She takes the Carhartt off his shoulders and throws it at the chair, and misses.

body: “It’s Saturday,” she says. “Say it again.”
He says it again — *I want you* — standing in the middle of her floor with his coat on the boards, and it’s as true now as it was three nights ago, truer, and she shuts her eyes to hear it.

“Also,” she says, with both palms flat on his chest, “I believe I owe somebody for the second quarter.” She walks him backward to the end of the mattress and pushes, gently, and he sits. “I said I reward that sort of behavior. I keep my word. Sit there. Rewards take a minute.”

The heater in the corner still doesn’t heat. Sol came Thursday with a wrench and a cigarette and did something to it with both, and since then it ticks — every few seconds, a small dry sound of metal making up its mind — and puts out nothing at all. Skye says it’s counting down to something. She won’t say what.

She has his flannel on, and nothing under it that he can see, and she sits cross-legged in the middle of the mattress in the lamplight with the white phone in both hands, scrolling with her thumb. She’s been on the bishops’ website. Tomorrow he’ll stand up for the Gospel at the 9:30, and she wanted to have read it first.
“Listen,” she says, and reads it to him.

body.title: usccb.org — Readings for Sunday, January 17, 2010 — John 2:1–11
body.text: Now there were six stone water jars there for Jewish ceremonial washings, each holding twenty to thirty gallons. … “Everyone serves good wine first, and then when people have drunk freely, an inferior one; but you have kept the good wine until now.”

body: “Your guy’s first miracle,” Skye says, “is a bar trick.”
He opens his mouth.

“No. Six jars.” She holds up the phone at him like a bid at an auction. “Twenty to thirty gallons each. Six times twenty is a hundred and twenty. Six times thirty is a hundred and eighty. I’m in *College Algebra*, Jack. Call it a hundred and fifty gallons of the good stuff, at the end of the night, after everybody’s had plenty.” She lowers it. “Somebody drove home from that.”
“John doesn’t call them miracles,” Jack says. “He calls them signs.”
“A sign of what? That he’s fun at parties?”
“That he’s there. And nobody at the party knew where it came from,” Jack says. “Only the servants. The ones who filled the jars.”
“The crew always knows.” She doesn’t even look up. “The producer’s the last to find out. That part I believe.”
“Read the end again.”

She reads the end again, and this time she does the steward: the head of catering at a hotel ballroom, holding a glass up to the light and appalled to his shoes, *everyone serves good wine first*. Halfway through the line her voice runs out. She scrolls back up with her thumb. Her lips move over the top of the page, where it says what kind of party it was.
“Oh,” Skye says. “It’s a *wedding*.”
He has stood for this Gospel every January of his life, in a pew at St. Brigid’s with his mother’s elbow in his side, and until now it was never about him.
She looks up from the phone at him sitting on the end of her bed in his jeans, and her mouth comes up at one corner, slowly, because she found it herself.
“So *you’re* the good wine.”
He laughs. He can’t help it, and he doesn’t try.
She puts her thumb under the last line and turns the screen around so he can see it. “*Until now*,” she says. “It says *now*.”
“It says *until*.”

She laughs at that — at him, at herself, at the bishops — and puts the phone face down on the floor by the lamp, and the argument goes down with it, unfinished, the way she likes to leave the good ones.
Then she gets up on her knees on the mattress, in his flannel, and pushes her hair back off her face with both hands and holds it there, and looks at him.

“Monday you got to look,” she says. “Lamp on. I want my turn. Call it your reward.” Her mouth tips. “Call it mine.” She lets her hair go. The dare is still in it, and something under the dare that she doesn’t dress up. “Let me see you, Jack.”

His shirt has been on her floor since the door. The jeans are easy; the jeans have been on her floor before, and on the floor of the Saab. The last thing is his to take off. He stands up off the mattress into the cold outside the lamp, and takes it off himself, with his own hand, and lets it fall, and steps back into the light.

Every joke he owns comes up at once. He doesn’t use any of them. His face is hot to the ears, and his hands want something to do, and he doesn’t give them anything; he keeps them at his sides and lets her.

She looks. She takes her time — every bit as long as he took, and she doesn’t make a single crack about any of it — and when her eyes come back up to his face there is color all the way down her throat, into the open collar of his flannel. He has never seen her blush. He didn’t know she could.
“Okay,” she says, very quietly, like he’s answered something she asked a long time ago.
She opens the flannel and lets it go off her shoulders behind her, and holds out her hand, and he comes down into the circle of the lamp with her.

There’s nothing on either of them anywhere. That’s new. Skin to skin the whole length of them, her cold feet and her warm mouth and all of it in between, so much of her that for a while he can’t find the edge of anything. Her heart going against his ribs. The cold of the room on his back and the heat of her under him, and the lamp on both. On Monday the line was a strip of cotton. Tonight there’s no cloth left in the bed to be the line. There’s only the thing itself, and a word, and the word is his to say.
And she starts to ask him for it.

Not *now* — she’s spent *now* — and not *when*. She asks for what. She has her face over his in the lamplight, where he can watch her mean it, and she starts to say it in her own words, the plain grown-up words for it, with her eyes on his: Skye, wanting him, all of him, tonight.

He wants it. He has said so to her face; he has said more than that, at two in the morning with his back against a furnace in Ohio, and she has every word of it. None of what he wants is a secret from him anymore. And this afternoon, in a coat closet with a card on the door that says KNOCK (gently), a priest had him say her name.

choices.text: *Say no before she finishes asking. Then stay.*
choices.key: Saturday night at Del Playa, with nothing left between you, you said no before she finished asking — and stayed.
response: “No,” he says — into it, in the middle of her sentence, so that her asking and his answer arrive in the room together and tangle in the lamplight.
She stops with her mouth open on the rest of it.

He doesn’t move. That’s the other half, and the harder one. He doesn’t roll away from her or reach for a blanket or a joke; he stays exactly where he is, all of him against all of her, and lets her feel it — that the no is there, and the wanting is there, and they’re the same size.

And Skye laughs. It comes up out of her against his stomach, surprised, a laugh he hasn’t heard from her yet: helpless. She’s been beaten to her own line, in her own bed, with the lamp on, by a boy from Ohio with no clothes on, and she drops her face into his neck and laughs there until the mattress shakes, and doesn’t let go of him once to do it.

choices.text: “Not that. Not without a wedding. You found it yourself.”
choices.key: Saturday night at Del Playa, with nothing left between you, you told her plainly: not without a wedding.
response: She finishes asking. He lets her; he owes her that much, to hear all of it. Then he takes her face in his hands, so that she has to stay where he can see her.
“Not that,” he says. “Not without a wedding.” And because it’s true, and because it was her thumb under the line: “You found it yourself.”
It’s his reason, start to finish, and she read it to him off the bishops’ website an hour ago doing a caterer.

Her mouth opens, ready for him, sure of itself. Nothing comes out of it. Her eyes go to the floor by the lamp, where the phone is lying on its face with the Gospel still lit underneath it, and come back to him, and she puts her fingers over his mouth, as if he might say it again and she couldn’t stand it twice.

choices.text: *Hold her. Forehead to hers. Say it there.*
choices.key: Saturday night at Del Playa, with nothing left between you, you held her and said no with your forehead against hers.
response: She finishes asking, and he doesn’t answer. He gets his arms all the way around her instead and holds her against him hard, her ribs against his, her breath pushed out of her in a laugh she didn’t mean. He puts his forehead to hers. Close enough that her eyes are all there is.
“No,” he says, there. “I want you. And no.”

Her eyes close. She doesn’t pull back to argue. She breathes out against his mouth, and he feels her hands come up off the blankets and go into his hair at the back of his head, and hold it, as if the no were something she could keep him still for.

choices.text: *Let it go to the very edge. Say it when there’s nothing left but saying it.*
choices.key: Saturday night at Del Playa, with nothing left between you, you let it go to the very edge before you said no.
response: He doesn’t answer her. He kisses her instead, and she takes it for the other answer, and nothing in the room is arguing with anything.

It goes on. Her weight moving, her breath going ragged at his ear, his name in it, the lamp on all of it and nowhere to hide from what either of them wants. They go by the place where he stopped on Monday, and he feels them go by it, and he lets them. Past it. Out past where he has any business being, the way the swell lifted over the reef at dawn when it felt the bottom: all of it standing up together, the sea gone tall and still for one second before it broke. Her face right there under his, open, waiting for the next thing in the world to happen.
And there, with nothing left but saying it, he says it.
*No.*
It takes all the breath he has. It comes out of him barely a word, hoarse, hardly louder than her breathing. Nothing else happens. It holds.

s12a.slug: SUNDAY · 12:40 AM · DEL PLAYA, HER ROOM

body.text: “You said it before I got there,” she says, into his neck, delighted and furious in one breath.
“A wedding,” she says, back to him, through his fingers, trying the word for weight.
She keeps her forehead where it is.
Her breath goes out of her. “That was *later*,” she says, with her eyes shut, like a girl who has caught him dealing off the bottom of the deck.

body: She takes it to the letter. That one thing is out of the bed, and nothing else is, and neither of them reaches for the lamp.

So it goes on, in the full light, and that’s what’s new and nearly more than he can stand: there is nowhere to put his face. In December there was the fog on the Saab’s windows. Last time there was the dark after she reached over him and put the lamp out. Tonight there’s a sixty-watt bulb under a paper shade and the two of them in it with nothing on, and she watches him want her and lets him watch her back, and she learns him the way she learned the stars for a voice-over, fast and thorough and showing off a little, and every time she comes up to the line she stops there exactly — not short of it, at it — and lets him feel where it is, and starts again. Once, at the worst possible moment, she does the steward at him — appalled, a glass held up to the lamp, *you have kept the good wine* — and he laughs so hard he has to turn his face into the pillow, and she laughs at him laughing, and then neither of them is laughing. The blankets go over the edge of the mattress onto the floor and stay there. The cold of the room comes in over everything the lamp doesn’t reach and raises the hair on her arms, and she says it’s Sol’s fault, and pulls him closer to fix it, and it isn’t any colder after that.
It doesn’t cool, and it isn’t let go anywhere. It’s the longest she has kept him there, and the most of him there has ever been to keep.
In the corner the heater ticks, counting down to whatever it’s counting down to, and doesn’t get there.

Much later the cold wins. She hangs over the edge of the mattress and drags one blanket up off the floor by its corner and gets it over both of them, badly, and lies down with her cheek on his chest and her knee across him, and there’s just the surf through the black glass, coming up the beach below Del Playa and going back.
“What did you do in there all that time?” she says. “This afternoon.”
He could tell her any of it. Most of it is his and the priest’s. He tells her the part that’s hers.

“He gave me something to do. A decade — the Our Father and ten Hail Marys. For you, by name.” His hand is in her hair. “I put it in where it says *us*. *Pray for* —” He stops, because it isn’t a story, it’s a prayer, and you don’t do a prayer for an audience. “Skye. I said Skye. Every time.”

She lifts her head off his chest. She props her chin on her fist on his breastbone and looks at him in the lamplight, and her face is open, and she leaves it that way while he looks back. As far as he can tell, no one has ever prayed for her by name before.
“Amen,” she says, late, and puts her face down into his shoulder to say the rest. “Late counts.”

She falls asleep first, in the middle of a sentence about Dale and the quarters, her knee still over him. He reaches down past the mattress and switches off the lamp, and the room is dark, and over them the black window has no stars in it and no rain yet, only the cloud, low and close and coming. He lies there and listens for it and doesn’t, quite, sleep.

journal.title: Skye Callender
journal.text: Skye Callender, two Ls. Wouldn’t give me a last name — said *Out* — till she texted it to me on the floor in Denver. Met her in a window seat in Montecito, reading O’Connor for a part and had the grandmother exactly backwards. Acts — since she was eleven. Starts here in January: spring, undeclared. She’s declared enough, she says. Doesn’t drink where there are phones. Drives a dented ’91 Saab she says is Swedish. It’s GM. Walked into the Pacific in November like it was a bath, and dared me in after her in my clothes. Asked to kiss me — out loud. She was the one who stopped, in the grandmother’s voice. Typed herself into my phone as SKYE (MISFIT), and called herself from it. Took ten hours to answer my correction. Work, she said — a carpet and a wall. Her car’s an orphan now, and it’s my fault. Nearly three hours at the Starlite, a truck stop up the 101, with Nonna’s pie on the table. Cast me as the Bible salesman. Wanted to know what believing is like — not what I believe. Wants me to miss her a reasonable amount. Get the window, she said. Kissed me again against the Saab in the lot. Slower. On purpose. She was the one who stopped — her thumb on my mouth. She’s on TV. *Sweetwater*, Thursdays at nine: she plays Cassidy, the nice one. Gina screamed. I explained GM to her. In her own car. Thanksgiving: texted me the whole drive from Pittsburgh. Spent it at her mother’s place in Studio City; the parrot says ‘momager.’ Told me not to watch her show. Wants me to be specific. We’re friends on Facebook now — one mutual friend: Theo, who knows everybody. Saturday night she called. Three hours on the porch. Made me do my family. Asked what Advent is. Asked if the TV part matters. Fell asleep in the middle of the Madonna. Monday she drove two hours from LA to sit in a car with me for two more, and set an alarm so she’d leave. Watched the President with the sound off and read his face like a script. Her phone learned a trick in September; she’s still not over it. Gives every truck on the 101 a whole life in three sentences. Knows every word of ‘Thunder Road.’ The tape deck finally let go of *Rumours*. Invited me to LA; I work Saturdays. Doesn’t take people home. Saturday, in daylight, on a rock above the tide pools: fractions, for the placement test. I drew her a pie. Sharks were a lie. I told her a saint broke in. Drove me to Burbank in the rain to be her cousin from Ohio. Everybody on a set wants something from her; she smiles for every phone. Plays a preacher’s daughter who forgives a thief. She played it dry. Washed a borrowed dress in a laundromat at one in the morning; it lived. Thinks the Immaculate Conception is the other one. Took the math test with forty kids and nobody looked at her once. Doesn’t take people home. Took me home. Lives on Del Playa, in a house with a darkroom she isn’t allowed in and two boards under the porch the boys won’t let on the rack — she’ll live there in January. On her bed I said no. She stopped everything and asked me why, and we talked till it got light. I told her it’s a no right now. She said she can work with that. Picked my present for the church party: a Magic 8-Ball. Every answer’s a line reading, she says. Her car died in Buellton; I pushed. She’s seen Our Lady of Guadalupe on every taco truck in the Valley and thought she was a brand. Friday night she took my ‘right now’ apart, point by point, with visual aids, and made a very good case. It’s still right now. I said no again, and she stopped right there and nowhere else. Came to the Anchor in my shirt; Gloria rated her boysenberry. She’s going to ask every day, she says. It’s in her calendar. Slept at her house. Just slept. She says that doesn’t happen. Taught me to surf at Ellery on Gaudete Sunday. I’m terrible. I go home in six days. She isn’t counting. Played Hale in her car from my description. Made me answer the question I couldn’t at the Starlite. Thursday at one in the morning, no moon at all, she drove the bluff with the lights off. Not before Christmas, she said — Christmas and New Year’s and long distance are too much for something new. When I get back we’re dating. Officially. A whole thing. She counted. GM is killing Saab. I’m on the hook. Christmas week: Theo’s known her since they were eleven — his father’s company makes her show. She calls him Ted; nobody else does. She saw us walk into the Hallorans’ together and hid behind a ficus. “Peace mission” was for him. He ran into her at a party in the hills on the twenty-second, and she says he knows. She had me do the weather barefoot in the snow. Seventeen days; she’s not counting. Christmas morning my family found her — Gina gave me her show on DVD. They know her as the nice one. She wants it on her headstone. The day after Christmas my whole family watched season two of her show. She was eighteen, in a blazer, on a dock. She’s good — Dad said so, and she says nobody says good. Nonna prays for Cassidy now. She bought Chesterton used on Ventura without knowing it was my book, and wants to know who picked midnight. The Monday after Christmas she called, and we talked till my phone died. New Year’s Eve she watched my ball drop on the East Coast feed at nine her time and texted, so she’d be at midnight with me. Then she had her own, at three in the morning mine, from a locked den in the hills. I told her I called Ted *Ted*. She says he’s right: that one’s hers. She has my flight home written on her hand. She read Matthew 2 because I said Sunday was Epiphany; Herod is a jealous showrunner. OFFICIALLY, in eyeliner, on a sign at the rope at Santa Barbara, in sunglasses at night. A girl from my flight filmed it, and by morning it was on a gossip blog. Skye put the still on her own Facebook herself. Her people wanted lunch: her mother, Debbie, who manages her, and her publicist, Corinne. The rules: no pictures, ‘a friend from school,’ February. Take the airport down. She took it down. There was a folder with my last name on it, and she pushed it back without opening it. At a gas station in Buellton she took the first picture of the two of us herself, at arm’s length, and put it up instead. Then she changed her status herself and made me say yes to it on her phone — the first thing anybody ever watched her do that nobody wrote. Monday she came to the Fishbowl and argued with me about a rose. My pie got her out of remedial math. Tuesday she taught me stick in an empty lot — a voice for every stall. I do a bad Frank. We argued Conan. She posted a picture of me stalling. The radio, at 2:31: Haiti. At midnight she took the picture down — not for Corinne. Wednesday in the Brick she explained the plates under Haiti from her Oceanography book, read me Milton off the front of *Frankenstein*, and fell asleep on my shoulder. At the Haiti table she borrowed Becca’s apron and was Cassidy for twenty dollars a name, and asked me where God was at 4:53. Met Laney. Met everybody. Corinne wanted a statement; she told her the girl at the table was right about the pictures, and hung up. That night she asked me to say one for them, from her. ‘Saturday.’ Thursday Margot interviewed her at the Anchor; she says I’m the same in every room. Saturday at dawn she taught me again, inside the Point. Still very bad at it. She posted it and kept it up. She came to Sully’s and learned the Who Dat. Laney took a shot at her; she had it handled, she says, and I didn’t let her finish, and she says she’ll reward that sort of behavior. In the Saab I told her some about Lena — that we were close in the fall. She heard more than I said. She drove me to confession, and went back to Sully’s without me. Saturday night she read me Sunday’s Gospel off her phone.

s13.slug: SUNDAY · 9:30 AM · ST. BRENDAN THE NAVIGATOR — CANA
body: In the night the cloud came in off the Channel and stopped against the hills in one low lid, the first weather of the year. He left Del Playa at half past eight with Skye asleep across the whole of the bed and the white phone still in her hand, and wrote *930 mass. st brendans at noon* on the back of the Oceanography syllabus from his bag and stood it against her alarm clock, and stood in the doorway a while longer than he had time for. He walks up through the Grove with the Carhartt zipped over yesterday’s shirt, and the eucalyptus are restless over the path, dropping bark in long strips. It isn’t raining. It looks like a sky that’s thinking about it.

The 9:30 is the Newman crowd’s Mass. Gus is up at the organ in the ship’s-wheel sweater; beside him Clare Dominguez has a violin under her chin, tuning, the 49ers cap off for church, and Kevin has taken the end of the front pew where he can hand her the music, which he does twice before she needs it. Joey, nineteen today, is telling Tyler Brandt so in the third pew, and Tyler already knows. Peter Haddad has the usher’s badge. Mrs. Fitch has her end of the fourth pew, as she has had it since before any of them were born.

Lena’s Mass is the nine o’clock at night. She’s here anyway, two pews ahead of him on the Lady’s side, with Julian, her hair up and the Haiti clipboard on the kneeler, and at the end of their pew four long-handled collection baskets lean against the wall with HAITI on an index card taped to each handle in her printing. The baskets tell him why. He didn’t pick the pew. It’s where there was room.

Becca reads the first reading. She reads it the way she says everything, straight out, Idaho-flat and unembarrassed: *No more shall people call you “Forsaken” … But you shall be called “My Delight.”* Jack has been carrying the same picture since Thursday, a TV picture of one runway and a fence and the crates stacked high on the wrong side of it, and *Forsaken* goes to it the minute she says it. *My Delight* hasn’t got anywhere to go yet.
Kenzie sings the psalm. Tyler reads Corinthians — *different kinds of spiritual gifts but the same Spirit* — as though he’d like to sign everybody up for at least one.

Osei reads the Gospel himself, in the green, with his weight off the bad leg. *When the wine ran short, the mother of Jesus said to him, “They have no wine.”* He reads it all the way down: the six stone jars, the servants filling them to the brim, the headwaiter who doesn’t know where it came from. The last time Jack heard those verses it was a little after ten last night, in another voice.
Osei doesn’t go up into the pulpit. He comes down to the foot of the step with his hands folded.

“Mary notices before anybody has said a word,” he says. “She does not fix it — she has no wine either. She tells him, and she tells the servants to do whatever he tells them, and then she goes back to the party, which I think is the hardest thing anybody does in this Gospel.”

He goes back up the step, and before the Creed he turns at the ambo. “The second basket today is for Haiti. Miss Broussard has the baskets, and she will count them twice. And Yaw has a generator now.” Half the church heard about Yaw on Wednesday, and the sound they make isn’t applause, because it’s church, but it’s next door to it.

At the offertory Gus starts the Haugen, and Clare comes in a bar late and then exactly right, and Lena and Julian and Peter take the long baskets down the pews. Julian takes Jack’s side. The basket comes along the pew at the end of its pole; Jack puts in what’s left of Thursday’s tips, folded twice, and Julian, at the far end of the handle, gives him the same small nod he gives everybody, and moves on to the next row.

At the sign of peace Joey goes up and down his pew shaking every hand in reach and two that aren’t, and Becca, across the aisle, reaches over and gives Jack hers, a ranch handshake, firm, *Peace be with you*, and means nothing by it but peace. Two pews up Lena turns to the pew behind hers, and gives her hand to a woman in a Saints scarf and to the woman’s little boy, and turns back to the front.
At the Lamb of God the pews begin to empty forward, one by one, from the front. Two pews up Julian stands to let Lena out, and sits back down, as he does every Sunday, with his hands on his knees.
Yesterday at ten to four Jack was absolved in a closet forty feet behind him. He knows what he’s been since last night, and he isn’t going up that aisle on the strength of not thinking about it.

journal.title: Fr. Gabriel Osei
journal.text: Newman chaplain. Kumasi, Ghana. Used to be a doctor. Limps and doesn’t mention it. Plays chess like he’s got all night and highlife like the neighbors owe him money. Told me a proverb about funerals. I laughed. That was apparently the point. Said Nonna’s Mass himself at the 12:10, like he promised. Gave me a card for her: ‘A grandmother likes paper.’ Blessed Hale’s deaf dog with his hand on its ribs, where it could hear. Finished Hale’s limerick for him. Laughed for a full minute at Becca’s crab. All Souls, at the book: ‘Write them all. He has a large book and a long memory.’ Saturday, behind the screen, one question: do I want to stop seeing her, or stop what happens. Change the hour. Keep her in the daylight. The Advent party: got the spray tan. Confiscated the mistletoe — he requested. At the sink he told me about the waiting room in Kumasi. His door is the one with the light on. Saturday, behind the screen: love wills the good of the other — and that’s why it’s dangerous. Gaudete: rejoice is a command. Wednesday, behind the screen: I’m not avoiding the occasion, I’m scheduling it. Distance is a mercy; use it. Blessed us both for the road on the Newman steps. Come back. The first day back I gave him Father Dom’s message: we’ll see. He laughed. I told him I went at home. The night of the earthquake he asked the bishop if he could spare an old doctor. The bishop couldn’t spare a young priest. His friend Yaw from medical school is in Port-au-Prince — alive, operating in a parking lot. Saturday at three-thirty the light was on. Sunday he read Cana. Yaw has a generator now.

choices.text: *Go up with your arms crossed over your chest.*
choices.key: On the Sunday of Cana you went up with your arms crossed for a blessing.
response: He gets into the line behind the woman in the Saints scarf and her little boy, with his arms crossed over his chest, right hand to left shoulder, the way the nuns at St. Brigid’s taught the second grade to go up before they were ready.

When he reaches the front Osei looks at the arms and lifts his free hand over Jack’s head instead of the Host, and makes the cross in the air. “May almighty God bless you.” His face is kind and has nothing else in it. Nothing in it has been in the closet.

On the way back he forgets to take his arms down. Lena is coming back along the side aisle with her hands folded, and her eyes go to his crossed arms, and up to his face, and then she’s past him to her pew, where Julian stands to let her in. In his own pew Jack uncrosses his arms and kneels.

choices.text: *Stay in the pew. Let the line go by.*
choices.key: On the Sunday of Cana you stayed in the pew and let the line go by.
response: He keeps his seat and moves his knees for the people going out past him. Joey goes by with “Excuse me, Jack, sorry, excuse me” at a volume meant for the upper deck.
Then it’s only him in his pew, and two rows up only Julian in his, both of them sitting, and the line going up the middle without them.

Lena’s line comes back along the side aisle past the end of his row. She sees the pew empty except for him, and him sitting in it, and her step doesn’t change, but her eyes stay on him a moment past the end of the pew. Then she’s past, and back in her own pew, kneeling, beside the man who never goes up.

choices.text: *Kneel. Say Nonna’s prayer for the ones who can’t go up — all the way to the end this time.*
choices.key: On the Sunday of Cana you knelt and said your grandmother’s prayer all the way through.
response: He kneels while the pew empties around him and shuts his eyes and starts it, the one Nonna taught him at the kitchen table for the Sundays you can’t go up. *My Jesus, I believe that You are present in the Most Holy Sacrament.* He gets to *come at least spiritually into my heart*, and Kenzie starts the communion hymn over his head, and he keeps going under it this time, all the way. *I embrace You as if You were already there, and unite myself wholly to You. Never permit me to be separated from You.*
“Amen,” he says, and opens his eyes.

Lena is passing the end of his pew, coming back along the side aisle with her hands folded, and from where she is she must have seen him on his knees with his lips moving. She looks at him straight for the length of one step, and then at the floor ahead of her, and goes on to her own pew.

s14.slug: SUNDAY · 10:50 AM · ST. BRENDAN’S, THE COURTYARD
body: The sprinkler under the olive tree, which hasn’t worked since anybody can remember, picks the end of the 9:30 to work. It comes on with a cough and throws one long arc across the flagstones, and Peter Haddad, carrying a folding table out of the hall, takes it across both shoes and stands there holding the table while it comes back the other way and gets him again. It quits. Peter sets the table down in the wet and says, to the olive tree, “Thank you, Lord.”

Over the courtyard wall the sky has come down low and gray to the Channel, and the wind smells like weather. Nobody believes it yet. The tables go up in a row: Coffee & Donuts, the urn, the second basket’s Haiti count on a clipboard, and in the middle, on a card table of its own, Mrs. Fitch’s sheet cake with blue piping around the edge and blue writing across the middle, HAPPY 19TH JOEY — AD MULTOS ANNOS, and a plate of lemon bars beside it. “Lemon bars are for the people who don’t like cake,” Mrs. Fitch tells Tyler Brandt, who has taken one of each. “There are always some.”
Joey stands in front of his cake with both hands over his mouth.

Father Osei, in his clerics, the vestments left in the sacristy, lifts his coffee cup like a baton and starts it himself, in Latin, in a voice that doesn’t sound like the one he uses at the altar: *Ad multos annos.* The Newman crowd comes in under him, Kenzie on a harmony of her own, Tyler a half beat behind, Gus humming the bass from the hall door, Mrs. Fitch moving her lips without committing. *Ad multos annos.* They go around it three times, and Joey is crying by the second, at full volume, which is the only volume Joey has.
“In eight *years*!” he tells the courtyard. “Eight years, and you’ll all have to call me Father, and I’ll remember who sang flat!”

He comes at Jack through the crowd with his arms out and gets him around the neck. “Jack! JACK. Nineteen! Did you sing? I didn’t hear you sing.” Jack says he sang. “Sing it again. Sing it in my ear.” Jack sings two words of it in his ear, and Joey lets go, satisfied, and is gone to the next neck.
“*Ad multos annos* means many years, Joseph,” Father Osei tells him, when the singing has stopped. “Not all of them at once. Sit down before you fall down.”
From the cake table Lena says, “*Ad multos annos*, cher,” and kisses him on the cheek, and Joey has to sit down on the cooler.

Becca has the knife. She cuts the cake into pieces with a ruler’s eye and lays them on paper plates, and Osei comes down the line carrying them two at a time. He puts one in Jack’s hand without stopping — a corner piece, more frosting than cake — and goes on to Clare with the other.

“Is Skye coming?” Becca says, over the cake. “I saved her a piece with a rose on it.” She shows him: one blue rose, the only one on the cake, cut out whole with its piece of cake around it and set aside on a plate of its own.
“She’s picking me up at noon. She’s driving to LA.”

“Then it’ll have to travel.” Becca lifts it onto two napkins, and folds them over the top without touching the rose, and hands the bundle across the table to him. “Keep it flat. It’s buttercream; it’ll slide if you tilt it.” She thinks of something. “And tell her the apron misses her.”

Kevin and Clare are at the end of the coffee table with Styrofoam cups, her violin case at her feet from the 9:30. Clare’s four brothers called her at halftime yesterday, Kevin reports, all four of them on one speakerphone in San Jose, to yell about Arizona.
“They had money on Arizona,” Clare says. “They’re idiots. I love them.” She takes the lid off her coffee. “The youngest one cried.”
“I explained concussions to her yesterday,” Kevin tells Jack. “For nine minutes. She timed it.”
“Eleven,” Clare says. “It was interesting.” She seems to mean that, and Kevin seems to know she does, and to be a little unsettled by it.
Kevin smiles at her. It’s a good smile; it’s the team-captain one, and he means it to be.
The wind comes over the wall and lifts the stack of napkins off the Coffee & Donuts table, and Tyler and Peter go after them across the wet flagstones, and Becca puts the sugar bowl on what’s left.
In Jack’s pocket the RAZR goes, and goes again. It’s ten to two in Youngstown, after Mass and the ham.

s15.slug: SUNDAY · 12:05 PM · OCEAN ROAD, OUTSIDE ST. BRENDAN’S — THE SAAB
body: The cloud has come all the way down to the Channel since Mass and is sitting on it, flat and gray out to where the islands were this morning, and the wind has turned around. It comes up Ocean Road off the water now instead of down off the hills, cold, smelling of salt and of something wet that hasn’t happened yet, and it gets under the Carhartt.

The Saab is at the curb with its top up for once, for the freeway. Across the back seat lies a garment bag with a dress in it that came up from Beverly Hills by messenger on Friday and that she still hasn’t unzipped, and on the dash, sliding a little every time a truck goes by, *Oceanography 1*. She’s going to read the chapter on refraction in the bathroom at the party, she says, so she has something to think about while she smiles.
He hands Becca’s rose in through the window, flat, as instructed, in its two napkins.
Skye unfolds it on her knee. “From the apron girl?”
“She saved it for you. She says the apron misses you.”

Skye eats the rose first. She takes it off the top whole with her fingers and puts it in her mouth, and shuts her eyes, and chews blue buttercream on Ocean Road at noon on a Sunday. “I’m going to write her a letter,” she says, with her mouth full. “On paper. With a stamp. She’s going to love it so much.”
She gets out to say goodbye properly and leans on the passenger door beside him with her sunglasses on, though there isn’t a scrap of sun. She has his flannel on over a T-shirt.
“That’s my shirt.”

“It’s going to a party.” She pulls the cuffs down over her hands. “It’s never been to Beverly Hills. It’s going to hate it. I’ll take it off in the parking garage and leave it in the car to wait for me, like a dog.”
“You could’ve asked me,” he says. “To come.”

“I know.” She doesn’t pretend she didn’t think about it. “You’d hate it, and I’d watch you hate it, and I’d leave, and Corinne would kill us both.” She puts her shoulder against his. “Everyone I know is going to be in that room. Everyone who’s ever signed anything with my name on it. They’re all going to tell me I look rested.”
“You don’t look rested.”

“I know. It’s your fault.” She tips her sunglasses down her nose to look at him over them, and pushes them back up. “Corinne has me at a table between a man from the network and a ficus. *Avatar* is going to win everything and everybody’s going to say they saw it in 3-D, sober.” She looks out at the gray water. “I’ll call you from the bathroom. That’s where the only real conversations at those things happen. Everybody’s in there crying or calling their mothers or doing something else in a stall, and nobody’s working.”

She’s in LA through Tuesday: a fitting Monday, ADR Tuesday — a booth, a pair of headphones, and a screen with her own face on it running up a staircase, and she has to breathe in time with herself till it matches. Wednesday she’s back. Wednesday she’ll be in the back row under the exit sign.
“Watch the Globes,” she says. “Count how many times I’m not on it.”
“Every time.”

“Then you’ll have a big number. You’re good with numbers.” A truck goes by and the wind it makes lifts the hair off her neck. She watches it go up the road toward the Grove. “I’ve been going to these since I was a kid,” she says. “I never minded leaving before.”

She turns and takes hold of the Carhartt by both sides of the open front and puts him back against the passenger door, and kisses him there, out in the open, with all of Ocean Road able to see — long, and slow, and getting less slow — her cold hands inside his coat on his ribs and her mouth tasting of buttercream, until he has stopped noticing the wind at all. And she ends it. She ends it on purpose, right where it’s best, and keeps hold of his coat for a second after, to make sure he noticed.

choices.text: “I’ll miss you.”
response: “Good,” Skye says. “A reasonable amount.”

She lets go of his coat and goes around the hood with her hand trailing over it, and gets in. He doesn’t wait to watch. He has the Brick and a chapter on tides, and he starts up Ocean Road with his hands in his pockets, and behind him the engine catches on the second try, and he hears her take it up through the gears toward the freeway, and the wind comes straight up the road at him off the gray water, colder than it’s been all year.

choices.text: “Steal me two mints.”
response: “Greedy,” Skye says, and once she’s in she points at him through the windshield and mouths it again.

He’s already walking. The Saab pulls out behind him and goes the other way, down toward the freeway, and he listens to it go until a truck covers it, and then there’s only the wind coming up Ocean Road with the weather in it and the olive tree over the courtyard wall turning its leaves over to the silver side, all at once, the way they do before it rains.

choices.text: *Fix her collar.*
response: The collar of the flannel has folded under at the back where his coat was in her fists. He reaches around and turns it out and smooths it down flat against her neck, and leaves his hand there, at the back of her neck, under her hair, where it’s warm.

She stands very still for it. She doesn’t say anything clever. She puts her own hand up over his and presses it there, and then takes it down and goes around to the driver’s side and gets in without a word, which he has never seen her do.

He stands on the curb in the cold coming up off the water and feels the place on his palm where her neck was, and the Saab pulls out behind him and goes, and he doesn’t turn around for it. He turns up his collar instead, and walks.

s16.slug: SUNDAY · 5:40 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE 4TH-FLOOR LOUNGE
body: He has spent the afternoon in the Brick with the Oceanography text open to a chapter on tides, and the sky is already the wrong gray when he comes out. The rain reaches the east stairwell about when he does: one fat drop on the landing window, then a handful, then the sound of all of it at once, the first of the year. The Carhartt goes dark across both shoulders on the last flight. By the fourth floor the glass is running and the building smells of wet eucalyptus, and on the stairwell door Priya’s newest laminate says PROPPED DOORS ARE A FIRE CODE VIOLATION, and under it, in pen, WEDGES ARE A LIFESTYLE.

The lounge door is propped on the wedge anyway, and the light and the noise of the television come out through the gap into the hall: a ballroom, a band playing somebody off, applause from a long way off. Under them, low, which it never is, Laney.
“…over Christmas, Margot. She told me over Christmas, and then —”
He puts a shoulder to the door, and the wedge gives, and the voice stops.

Laney is on the window seat with her knees up, her nails done in black and gold, the left thumbnail chewed back to the quick. Margot is in the armchair beside her with a laptop open on her knees and a legal pad on the arm. The window behind them is running. Laney sees him once, and that settles it. She unfolds from the seat, pockets her phone and crosses the room, and goes past him in the doorway so close that he gets her shampoo, coconut, and nothing else. On the sill her tea is still steaming, the string hanging over the rim.
“Laney,” he says.
Her flats go off down the hall carpet. The stairs take her.
“Is she —” Jack says.

“She has gone to watch the Golden Globes in a room with fewer of you in it,” says Margot, and turns her screen a few degrees away from his side of the room. She reaches over and takes Laney’s tea off the sill and drinks it, because it is hot and it is there.

On the television a woman in a column of silver is cutting between tables toward the stage, followed by a man whose only job, apparently, is her train. Jack watches the edges of the shot for a face that isn’t going to be there. Then the host, in a tuxedo, says something to a ballroom of the famous that makes the front tables laugh a second late. “He insults them and they love him,” Margot says, watching it. “It’s a power dynamic in a tuxedo.”
Doug is on the floor with his back against the couch and a bag of pretzels on his chest. “Dude,” he says, to Jack, upside down. “Is Skye *on*?”
“She’s not presenting,” Jack says. “She’s at a party after.”
Doug lets the pretzels settle. “*After*,” he says, reverently. “With the *Avatar* people. In the same room as the blue ones.”
“They don’t come blue,” Jack says.
“You don’t know that.” Doug eats a pretzel. “What do they eat at those, dude? Is it just one grape?”
“I’ll find out.”
“You have to. For the floor.”
Kevin asks, from the couch, whether the Globes are always this long.
“It is a four-hour lunch for sixty people with cameras,” Margot says. “Yes.”

Kevin, on the couch with his chemistry, has his BlackBerry buzz against the cushion. He turns it over and reads it, lays it face-down on the page, and goes on highlighting a line that is already yellow.

Margot has closed the laptop to a slit. “My column runs Thursday,” she says. “‘Front Stage.’ I have her: an evening, on the record, with the subject’s boyfriend as an unwilling witness in the dish pit. She says there is no backstage, only more stages. She also says you are the same in every room. Those are difficult claims to hold at once, and I would like to know which she’s lying about.”
“Which?” Jack says.
“Neither, I suspect, which is a hypothesis I resent.” She uncaps a pen. “What I lack is a control. One line from one of the rooms.”
“Do we get names?” Doug says. “Can I be, like, Douglas P.?”
“You will be ‘a friend,’” says Margot. “Possibly ‘a floor.’”

choices.text: “Tell them I’m load-bearing.”
response: Margot writes it down. “‘Load-bearing,’” she reads back. “A structural claim.”
“What does that mean?” Doug asks the ceiling.
“It means he holds up the roof, Douglas,” Margot says, “and doesn’t think it’s his job.” On the television the room laughs again, a second late, and the rain goes on at the window.

choices.text: “Tell them she’s right.”
response: Margot looks at him over the frames until the television has laughed twice. “That is not a quote,” she says. “That is a confession.”
“Is it going in?” Doug says.

“I’m thinking about it,” says Margot, and the pen stays where it is. Behind her the window runs with the first rain of the year, and on the screen somebody is being kissed on both cheeks by someone who has clearly just met her.

choices.text: “No comment.”
response: “That’s a comment, Costigan,” Margot says. “I’ll print it as one.”

Doug, from the floor, would like it noted that he has a comment, and that it is about the grape. Nobody takes him up on it. The ballroom applauds somebody, and the rain finds the gutter over the window and begins to pour.

body: The rain has settled in. It came on hard at dinner and then found its pace, and now it’s just the sound the night makes, steady on the window toward the Grove and loud in the downspout outside, and the eucalyptus breathing it out across the quad. 412 is dark. The light off the lamps on the walk comes up under the blind, wet and moving.

On Theo’s nightstand Hollis sits in his teacup, intact, HOLLIS down the shell in somebody else’s blue capitals, four days into his week. Theo has carried him to a pledge breakfast and a chapter dinner and back up the east stairs in the rain, at a walk, level, with an umbrella held over the cup and not over himself, and there is rain still drying in his hair.

Theo’s umbrella stands open between the beds, dripping a dark ring around itself, and the room smells like wet nylon and the eucalyptus he carried in on his shoes. Theo turns off his lamp. He’s half under before the room has finished going dark. Theo has always been able to sleep on command.
“How’s Hollis?” Jack says.
Out of the dark, very nearly asleep: “He’s thriving.”
Up on the closet shelf, where the glow from outside just reaches, Ma’s can sits on his own half, and across the divider the clean place where the duffel was is still clean.
The RAZR goes on his chest. He opens it with the screen turned in toward the wall, out of habit now, though Theo is asleep.
